title: Vector Databases

techniques.name: IVFFlat Index
techniques.q: Can I search only the nearest clusters?
techniques.what: IVF (inverted file) indexing groups vectors into clusters with k-means, each represented by a centroid. A query is first compared with the centroids, then only the vectors in the closest few clusters (the probes) are scanned. “Flat” means vectors inside each list are stored uncompressed, so distances within a list are exact.
use: Moderate datasets where fast index builds matter
Postgres with pgvector, when memory is tight
Batch-loaded data that doesn’t change much
metrics: number of clusters; pgvector suggests rows ÷ 1,000 up to 1M rows, √rows above
clusters scanned per query; higher = better recall, slower
k-means runs on the data present when the index is built
compress vectors inside lists to save memory
steps: Load representative data before building, since clusters are learned from it
Set lists to about rows ÷ 1,000 (up to 1M rows) or √rows beyond that
Start probes around √lists and tune for your recall target
Rebuild the index after large changes to the data
pitfalls: An index built on an empty or tiny table has poor clusters
Recall drops as new data drifts from the original clusters
Queries near cluster borders need more probes
techniques.cap: Faded clusters are never scanned. Raising probes trades speed for recall.

techniques.name: HNSW Index
techniques.q: Can I hop through a graph to the nearest neighbours?
techniques.what: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a layered graph. Upper layers are sparse with long links for coarse navigation; the bottom layer holds every vector with short links. A search enters at the top, greedily moves toward the query, and drops one layer at a time. It gives high recall at low latency and is the default index in most vector databases.
use: Low-latency, high-recall search where vectors fit in RAM
Data that grows continuously; no training step needed
General-purpose default when unsure
metrics: links per node; more = better recall, more memory (pgvector default 16)
candidate list while building; higher = better graph, slower build (default 64)
candidate list at query time; the main recall/latency dial (default 40)
assigned randomly per node; roughly log N layers
steps: Start with the defaults and measure recall on real queries
Tune ef_search at query time to reach your recall target
Budget memory: the graph links sit on top of the raw vectors
Expect slower builds and inserts than IVF
pitfalls: Memory-hungry: vectors and graph should fit in RAM
Heavy deletes and updates degrade the graph over time
Strict metadata filters can cut graph paths and lower recall
techniques.remember: Long hops on top, short hops at the bottom.
techniques.cap: Four hops and two layer drops reach the nearest vector without scanning the rest.

techniques.name: DiskANN
techniques.q: What if the index doesn’t fit in memory?
techniques.what: DiskANN, from Microsoft Research, stores a graph index (Vamana) and full-precision vectors on SSD and keeps only compressed vectors in RAM. The search walks the graph using the compressed codes, reads a handful of SSD pages per query, then re-ranks with full vectors. It serves billion-scale datasets from a single machine with modest RAM.
use: Hundreds of millions to billions of vectors
RAM costs that make in-memory HNSW impractical
Latency targets in milliseconds, not microseconds
metrics: a single-layer graph with long-range edges; few hops per query
a few page reads per query
exact distances on full vectors at the end
steps: Consider it when vectors × bytes exceeds the RAM you can afford
Use fast NVMe SSDs, since latency depends on random reads
Tune the search list size and beam width for recall versus I/O
Benchmark p95 latency under concurrent load, not single queries
pitfalls: Slower than in-memory HNSW at small scale
Index builds for very large datasets take a long time
Performance depends heavily on SSD quality
techniques.remember: Graph on SSD, compressed copy in RAM.
techniques.cap: 1B × 768 × 4 bytes ≈ 3.1 TB in RAM versus 1B × 32 bytes = 32 GB of codes.

techniques.name: Coarse-to-Fine Retrieval and Re-scoring
techniques.q: Can a cheap pass narrow things down before a precise one?
techniques.what: A multi-stage pattern, also called phased ranking or re-scoring. A cheap, approximate first layer (binary or compressed vectors, a coarse index) returns a generous candidate set. Each later layer is more precise and more expensive but sees far fewer items, ending with full-precision distances or a cross-encoder. Vector databases expose it as oversampling plus re-scoring.
use: Very large corpora with a strict latency budget
Quantized indexes that need a precise final score
Pipelines ending in an expensive re-ranker
metrics: binary or PQ vectors over the whole corpus → top 1,000
fetch more candidates than needed at early layers
recall@k and latency after each layer
steps: Measure the cheap layer’s recall at several candidate counts
Size each layer so the next one rarely misses a true match
Keep full-precision vectors available for the final rescore
Track latency per layer to find the bottleneck
pitfalls: Anything the first layer misses is lost for good
Extra layers add latency and moving parts
The name means different things in different products, so check what yours does
techniques.remember: Wide and cheap first, narrow and exact last.
techniques.cap: Candidate counts are typical examples. Tune them against measured recall.

techniques.name: Hybrid Search
techniques.q: How do I get meaning and exact matches together?
techniques.what: Run dense (vector) and sparse (BM25) search side by side and fuse the two result lists, usually with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which combines ranks rather than raw scores. Add metadata filters for date, tenant and permissions so results are both relevant and allowed.
use: Queries that mix meaning with codes, names or jargon
Enterprise search with permission filters
When neither vector nor keyword search alone reaches your recall target
metrics: exact terms via BM25 or SPLADE
applied before or after the vector search
steps: Index each chunk in both a vector index and a keyword index
Retrieve the top 50–100 from each and fuse with RRF
Apply permission and tenant filters before results leave the database
Re-rank the fused list and test on both kinds of query
pitfalls: Two indexes to keep in sync
Raw scores aren’t comparable across methods; use ranks or normalize
Post-filtering can leave too few results, so oversample or pre-filter
techniques.remember: Dense for meaning, sparse for words, fuse by rank.
techniques.cap: Documents found by both methods rise to the top. Scores are computed with k = 60.

cmp.best: Two indexes to keep in sync

techniques.name: Metadata Filtering
techniques.q: Can I search by meaning and still respect hard facts?
techniques.what: Combine vector similarity with structured conditions on each chunk, such as date, product, region, document type or version, so the top k are the nearest chunks that also match. Where the filter runs matters: after the vector search (post-filtering), before it with an exact scan (pre-filtering), or inside the index walk with payload indexes (filtered ANN). Access control and multi-tenancy are a separate technique, and extracting filters from a user’s words belongs to agentic retrieval in RAG Pipelines.
use: Questions scoped to a product, region, date range or document version
Catalogues and knowledge bases where a rare filter must still return a full top k
Replacing “please only use 2025 circulars” in the prompt with a guaranteed condition
metrics: share of chunks that match the filter; 0.5% means 10,000 of 20 lakh
ANN top k first, then drop non-matching; expected survivors = k × selectivity
find matching ids first, then score them exactly; cost grows with the matching count
the filter is checked during the graph walk (Qdrant, Weaviate ACORN, pgvector iterative scans)
a keyword, number or date index on a field; lets the planner estimate cardinality
fetch more candidates than k so enough survive a filter
steps: List the fields users filter on and store them as typed metadata at ingestion
Create payload or attribute indexes on those fields before the bulk load
Filter inside the vector query, not in application code after it
Measure recall@k and latency per selectivity band: broad, medium and rare filters
pitfalls: Post-filtering a top 10 with a rare filter returns few or no results
Pre-filtering a broad filter turns into a slow exact scan of most of the collection
Unindexed or inconsistent metadata (“MH” vs “Maharashtra”) silently drops matches
techniques.remember: Filter inside the search, index what you filter, test the rare filters.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Suraksha General, a fictional insurer, with 20 lakh chunks. Expected survivors of a post-filter = 10 × selectivity.

cmp.needs: Queries scoped by date, product, region or version
cmp.best: Post-filter recall collapse on rare filters

techniques.name: Multi-Tenancy and Access Control
techniques.q: Can one vector store keep every client’s data apart?
techniques.what: One vector store serves many customers (tenants) and many users, and every search must return only chunks the caller may see. Tenant isolation is a separate layer from document permissions: a namespace, collection or shard per tenant, a shared index with a tenant filter, or row-level security in the database. Document ACLs are synced from the source system, tenant-qualified, and enforced inside the query rather than asked of the model. Metadata filtering in general, and filtered-search recall, are covered by their own technique; this one is about who may see what.
use: A SaaS product serving many client companies from one vector store
Enterprise search where users see only the documents their groups may open
Regulated data (NBFC loan files, KYC, health records) that must be erasable per client
metrics: namespace or shard per tenant, shared index with a tenant filter, or database row-level security
taken from the verified token and set per request, never from the prompt or request body
groups or users allowed to read each chunk, prefixed with the tenant (t042:pune-credit)
how fast a revocation in the source system reaches the index: nightly, hourly or on change
in the query (filter before ranking), after retrieval, or only as a prompt instruction
deleting every chunk, cache and backup copy of a tenant when the contract or purpose ends
steps: Choose the isolation model per tier: namespaces for big or regulated clients, a shared index for the long tail
Take the tenant from the verified token and let the database enforce it (RLS, namespace or tenant index)
Store tenant-qualified ACLs on every chunk and filter by them inside the query
Sync ACL changes on events, red-team cross-tenant queries, and rehearse deleting a tenant
pitfalls: A tenant filter added by hand in app code is forgotten on one new endpoint
Group names such as “credit-ops” exist in many tenants, so an ACL check alone lets another client’s chunks through
A nightly ACL sync lets a revoked user read documents for up to a day
techniques.remember: Tenant from the token, enforced by the database. ACLs in the query, synced on change.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: LendStack, a fictional loan-servicing SaaS for 400 NBFC clients, with 2,400 access revocations a day.

cmp.needs: Many tenants or users in one store
cmp.best: Filters forgotten in app code; stale ACLs

techniques.name: Vector Compression (Scalar, Product and Binary Quantisation)
techniques.q: Can the index fit in a fraction of the RAM?
techniques.what: Vector compression stores fewer bits per dimension so a large index fits in RAM. Scalar quantisation maps each float32 to an int8 (4× smaller); product quantisation (PQ) splits the vector into sub-vectors and stores a one-byte codebook id for each (often 32–64× smaller); binary quantisation keeps only the sign of each dimension (32× smaller). Each step down loses some recall, which is won back by oversampling candidates from the compressed codes and rescoring them with full-precision vectors kept on SSD. This technique is about bytes per dimension; reducing the number of dimensions is covered in module 4, and multi-stage pipelines in general by Layered Approximate Search.
use: Corpora of crores of vectors where float32 would need hundreds of GB of RAM
Cutting the monthly bill of a managed vector database
Fast first-stage candidates before a precise rescore
metrics: 4× smaller; each dimension clipped to a range and mapped to 256 levels; recall loss usually about 1–2 points
vector split into m sub-vectors, each stored as a codebook id; needs training; 16–64× smaller
1 bit per dimension, 32× smaller, Hamming distance is very fast; works best on 1,000+ dims from models trained for it
fetch k × factor candidates from the compressed index, e.g. 40 for a top 10
re-rank candidates with original vectors, often read from SSD
recall at k against exact float32 search on your own queries
steps: Measure RAM, latency and recall at 10 with float32 as the baseline
Pick the encoding: int8 first, binary or PQ when RAM is the binding limit
Keep original vectors on SSD and rescore an oversampled candidate set
Tune the oversampling factor until recall is back within a point of the baseline
pitfalls: Binary quantisation on a small or unsuited embedding model, where recall collapses
Compressing without keeping the original vectors, so rescoring is impossible
Reporting speed-ups without measuring recall against exact search
techniques.remember: Fewer bits in RAM, full vectors on disk, oversample and rescore.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Bazaar Kart, a fictional marketplace, holds 2 crore product vectors of 1,024 dims.

cmp.needs: Indexes too big or costly for RAM

techniques.name: Choosing a Vector Store
techniques.q: Which vector database should we actually run?
techniques.what: Choosing a vector store is a product decision, not an algorithm choice: the index types covered elsewhere in this module (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) are available in most stores. The options fall into four families: a vector extension in a database you already run (Postgres with pgvector), a dedicated open-source engine (Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate), a managed serverless service (Pinecone and others) and an existing search engine (OpenSearch, Elasticsearch). The deciding constraints are usually scale, filtering and hybrid needs, where the data must live, how much operations time the team has, and cost at your size. Shortlist on those, then benchmark two finalists on your own data and queries.
use: Starting a first RAG or search product
Outgrowing an early prototype store
A data residency or audit requirement that rules options in or out
metrics: vectors now and in 2 years; pgvector is comfortable to about 1 crore on one node, engines scale out
metadata filters that keep recall, and BM25 plus vectors in one query
data in your own cloud account or an Indian region; audit and deletion
who patches, backs up, reindexes and gets paged
RAM, disk, requests and staff time per month
recall at 10 and p95 latency on your own queries with your filters
steps: Write down scale, filters, residency, latency target and ops budget
Shortlist two families that meet every hard constraint
Benchmark both on a sample of real documents and queries, with filters
Choose, and keep an export path: vectors and metadata in an open format
pitfalls: Choosing from a public benchmark that used different data, filters and hardware
Adding a new database when Postgres with pgvector would have served for years
Ignoring where the data must live until a compliance review blocks launch
techniques.remember: Constraints first, two finalists, benchmark on your own queries.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Suvidha Finance, a fictional NBFC, needs search over 1 crore chunks that must stay in its own cloud account.

chooser: We need fast index builds on a moderate dataset in Postgres
ivf
Use IVFFlat with lists ≈ rows ÷ 1,000 and tune probes for recall.
We want the lowest latency and highest recall, and the data fits in RAM
hnsw
Use HNSW and tune ef_search to hit your recall target.
We have billions of vectors and limited memory
diskann
Keep the graph and full vectors on SSD with compressed codes in RAM.
We have a huge corpus and a strict latency budget
las
Search cheap compressed vectors first, then rescore a shrinking candidate set.
Queries mix meaning with product codes or names
hybrid
Run vector and keyword search together and fuse the ranks with RRF.
Filtered searches return fewer than k results, or none, when the filter is strict
metafilter
Stop filtering after a small top-k: filter inside the search with payload indexes, or pre-filter and scan exactly when few chunks match.
Many client companies or users share one vector store
tenancy
Enforce the tenant in the database (RLS, namespace or tenant index), filter tenant-qualified ACLs inside the query, and sync ACL changes on events.
The vector index needs more RAM than you can afford
compress
Quantise the vectors (int8, binary or PQ), keep full vectors on SSD, and oversample then rescore to recover recall.
The team cannot agree which vector database to use
choosevs
List hard constraints (scale, filters, residency, ops, cost), shortlist two families, and benchmark both on your own queries.

import faiss, numpy as np

xb = np.load("chunks.npy").astype("float32")      # 2,000,000 × 384   #@1
faiss.normalize_L2(xb)            # unit length: inner product = cosine   #@1
d, nlist = xb.shape[1], 2000      # nlist ≈ rows ÷ 1,000   #@2

quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)  # holds the 2,000 centroids   #@2
index = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, d, nlist, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)   #@2
sample = xb[np.random.choice(len(xb), 200_000, replace=False)]   #@2
index.train(sample)               # k-means learns the centroids   #@2
index.add(xb)                     # each vector joins its nearest centroid's list   #@3

xq = embed(["How do I reset my UPI PIN?"]).astype("float32")   #@4
faiss.normalize_L2(xq)            #@4
index.nprobe = 45                 # ≈ √nlist lists scanned per query   #@4
D, I = index.search(xq, 10)       # exact distances inside ~45 of 2,000 lists   #@5

exact = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)      # brute force, for evaluation only   #@6
exact.add(xb)                     #@6
_, I_true = exact.search(xq, 10)  #@6
recall = len(set(I[0]) & set(I_true[0])) / 10   # recall@10   #@6
steps: Load and normalise the vectors
Load representative data first, because the clusters are learned from it. Unit-length vectors make inner product equal to cosine similarity.
Train the centroids
k-means on a sample learns nlist centroids. Two million rows ÷ 1,000 gives 2,000 lists; the picture uses 4.
Fill the inverted lists
Every vector is stored in the list of its nearest centroid. A list is scanned as a unit at query time.
Pick the nearest lists
The query is compared with every centroid, a cheap step, and the nprobe closest lists are chosen: 2 of 4 here.
Scan only those lists
Exact distances are computed inside the probed lists only: 16 of 32 vectors here, and 45 of 2,000 lists, about 2%, at full scale.
Measure recall
Compare with exact search on sample queries. If recall@10 is below target, raise nprobe; if it falls as data changes, rebuild.

import hnswlib

index = hnswlib.Index(space="cosine", dim=384)              #@1
index.init_index(max_elements=5_000_000, M=16,              #@1
                 ef_construction=200, random_seed=42)       #@1,3
# Each added vector draws a random top layer: P(layer ≥ 1) = 1/M   #@2
index.add_items(vectors, ids, num_threads=8)                #@2,3

index.set_ef(80)                  # ef_search: candidate list at query time   #@5
labels, distances = index.knn_query(query_vec, k=10)        #@4,5

# Memory: vectors 5M × 384 × 4 B ≈ 7.7 GB; bottom-layer links 5M × 32 × 4 B ≈ 0.64 GB   #@6
for ef in (40, 80, 160):                                    #@6
    index.set_ef(ef)                                        #@6
    got, _ = index.knn_query(sample_queries, k=10)          #@6
    print(ef, recall_at_10(got, exact_ids))                 #@6
steps: Set the graph parameters
M = 16 links per node on the upper layers and 32 on the bottom. ef_construction = 200 sets how widely each insert searches for neighbours.
Give each node a layer
Each insert draws a random top layer. With M = 16, about 1 node in 16 reaches layer 1 and 1 in 256 reaches layer 2, so upper layers are sparse.
Link each node to close neighbours
On every layer it belongs to, a new node links to close nodes found by an ef_construction-wide search. The sparse top layer ends up with long links.
Search greedily from the top
The query enters at the top layer's entry point and hops to whichever neighbour is closer, until none is, then drops a layer and repeats.
Widen the search on layer 0
The bottom layer keeps a list of ef_search candidates instead of one, which recovers neighbours a purely greedy walk would miss. The best k are returned.
Tune ef_search and budget memory
Recall rises with ef_search and needs no rebuild. For 5 million 384-dim vectors, links add about 0.64 GB on top of 7.7 GB of vectors.

import numpy as np, diskannpy

vecs = np.load("images_768d.npy", mmap_mode="r")   # 1,000,000,000 × 768 float32 ≈ 3.1 TB   #@1
diskannpy.build_disk_index(                                  #@2,3
    data=vecs, distance_metric="l2",   # unit vectors: L2 ranks like cosine   #@2
    index_directory="/nvme/idx",                             #@3
    graph_degree=64,                   # R: max edges per node in the Vamana graph   #@2
    complexity=100,                    # candidate list size while building   #@2
    search_memory_maximum=32.0,        # GB of RAM at search: sets PQ code size, ~32 B each   #@1,3
    build_memory_maximum=512.0, num_threads=0)               #@2

index = diskannpy.StaticDiskIndex("/nvme/idx", num_threads=16,   #@4
                                  num_nodes_to_cache=500_000)    # hot nodes near the entry   #@4
ids, dists = index.search(query_vec, k_neighbors=10,        #@5,6
                          complexity=100,  # L: candidate list, recall vs SSD reads   #@5
                          beam_width=4)    # SSD reads issued per round trip   #@5
# Results are ordered by exact distances from the full vectors already read   #@6
steps: Size the problem
1 billion × 768 dims × 4 bytes ≈ 3.1 TB, far beyond one server's RAM. Compressed PQ codes of 32 bytes each need only 32 GB.
Build a Vamana graph
One flat graph with at most R = 64 edges per node. Its pruning keeps some long-range edges, so a search needs few hops.
Split storage between SSD and RAM
Each node's full vector and neighbour list sit together in one 4 KB SSD sector. RAM holds only the PQ codes, plus a cache of hot nodes.
Start at the entry point
Every search begins at a fixed medoid. Cached nodes around it are served from RAM, which saves the first SSD reads.
Beam search over the SSD
Each round reads the best unvisited candidates by PQ distance, beam_width = 4 at a time. With L = 100 that is about 25 round trips.
Re-rank with the full vectors
The sectors already read contain full-precision vectors, so exact distances order the final 10 with no extra I/O.

import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder

emb = np.load("emb_f32.npy", mmap_mode="r")   # 1,000,000 × 1024 float32 = 4.1 GB, on SSD   #@1
bits = np.packbits(emb > 0, axis=1)           # 128 B per vector = 128 MB in RAM   #@1
s = 127 / np.abs(emb).max()                                   #@1
i8 = np.round(emb * s).astype(np.int8)        # 1 KB per vector = 1 GB in RAM   #@1

model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5")        # 1024 dims   #@2
q = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)            #@2
POP = np.array([bin(i).count("1") for i in range(256)], dtype=np.uint8)   #@2
ham = POP[bits ^ np.packbits(q > 0)].sum(axis=1)   # Hamming distance to every vector   #@2
c1 = np.argpartition(ham, 1000)[:1000]             # layer 1: 1,000,000 → 1,000   #@2

q8 = np.round(q * s).astype(np.int32)                          #@3
c2 = c1[np.argsort(-(i8[c1].astype(np.int32) @ q8))[:100]]     # layer 2: 1,000 → 100   #@3
c3 = c2[np.argsort(-(emb[c2] @ q))[:10]]                        # layer 3: exact, 100 → 10   #@4

ce = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")       #@5
scores = ce.predict([(query, texts[i]) for i in c3])            #@5
final = c3[np.argsort(-scores)]                # layer 4: ordered by relevance   #@5

exact = np.argsort(-(emb @ q))[:10]            # brute force, for evaluation only   #@6
recall = len(set(c3) & set(exact)) / 10        # measure on many sample queries   #@6
steps: Store three precisions
Binary codes (128 B) and int8 (1 KB) sit in RAM; full float32 vectors (4 KB) stay on SSD. For one million vectors: 128 MB, 1 GB and 4.1 GB.
Layer 1: Hamming scan
XOR and popcount against every binary code is very cheap. Keep a generous 1,000 candidates, because anything dropped here is lost for good.
Layer 2: int8 rescore
Integer dot products on the 1,000 candidates restore most of the precision. Keep the top 100.
Layer 3: exact rescore
Fetch 100 full vectors from SSD and compute exact cosine similarity. Keep the top 10.
Layer 4: cross-encoder
A cross-encoder reads the query and each passage together and orders the last 10 by relevance rather than by vector distance.
Measure recall per layer
Compare with exact search on sample queries. Retention multiplies: 0.97 × 0.99 × 1.0 ≈ 0.96 of the true top 10 survive.

import numpy as np
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder

docs = load_chunks()                   # each chunk: text, tenant, updated_at
bm25 = BM25Okapi([d.text.lower().split() for d in docs])            #@1
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")                      #@1
emb = model.encode([d.text for d in docs], normalize_embeddings=True)   #@1

query = "VPN error 809 on Windows"
allowed = np.array([d.tenant == user.tenant for d in docs])          #@2

sparse = bm25.get_scores(query.lower().split())                     #@3
dense = emb @ model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)          #@3
sparse[~allowed] = -np.inf; dense[~allowed] = -np.inf                #@2
top_s = np.argsort(-sparse)[:50]                                     #@3
top_d = np.argsort(-dense)[:50]                                      #@3

def rrf(*rankings, k=60):                                            #@4
    scores = {}                                                      #@4
    for ranking in rankings:                                         #@4
        for rank, i in enumerate(ranking, start=1):                  #@4
            scores[i] = scores.get(i, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)            #@4
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)              #@4

fused = [i for i in rrf(top_d, top_s) if allowed[i]][:20]           #@5
ce = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")            #@6
order = np.argsort(-ce.predict([(query, docs[i].text) for i in fused]))   #@6
final = [fused[j] for j in order[:5]]                                #@6
steps: Index every chunk twice
A BM25 index for exact terms and an embedding index for meaning. Both use the same chunk IDs and carry the same metadata.
Filter to what the user may see
The tenant filter is applied before ranking, so every candidate is one this user is allowed to read.
Retrieve from both
Dense search ranks D3 first and D1 second. BM25 ranks D1 first, because it contains the exact code 809.
Fuse ranks with RRF
Each list adds 1 ÷ (60 + rank). D1 gets 1/62 + 1/61 = 0.0325 and D3 gets 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0323. Raw scores are never compared.
Keep the fused top
Documents found by both methods rise to the top; documents found by only one follow. The top 20 go forward.
Re-rank and test both query types
A cross-encoder orders the final few. Evaluate code-style and meaning-style queries separately, since each method fails on a different kind.

                    ("doc_type", models.PayloadSchemaType.KEYWORD),       #@1
                    ("effective_from", models.PayloadSchemaType.DATETIME)]:  #@1
    client.create_payload_index(C, field_name=field, field_schema=kind)   #@1

    for c in chunks])                                                     #@2

flt = models.Filter(must=[                                                #@3
    models.FieldCondition(key="product", match=models.MatchValue(value="motor")),   #@3
    models.FieldCondition(key="region", match=models.MatchValue(value="MH")),       #@3
    models.FieldCondition(key="doc_type", match=models.MatchValue(value="circular")),  #@3
    models.FieldCondition(key="effective_from",                           #@3
                          range=models.DatetimeRange(gte="2025-04-01T00:00:00Z"))])  #@3

res = client.query_points(C, query=qvec, query_filter=flt, limit=10,     #@4
                          search_params=models.SearchParams(hnsw_ef=128)).points  #@4

n = client.count(C, count_filter=flt, exact=False).count   # about 10,000   #@5
# 0.5% of the collection: the planner scans those exactly via the payload index  #@5

# the anti-pattern: top 10 first, filter afterwards                        #@6
top = client.query_points(C, query=qvec, limit=10).points                  #@6
kept = [p for p in top if p.payload["region"] == "MH"]   # usually empty    #@6
steps: Index the fields you filter on

Every field a query will filter on gets a payload index: keywords for product, region and document type, a datetime index for the effective date. Create them before the bulk upload, so the HNSW graph is built with the extra links that keep filtered walks connected.
Store metadata with every chunk

Each chunk carries its structured facts as payload: motor, Maharashtra, circular, version 3, effective from 1 April 2025. Metadata that is missing or free text at ingestion cannot be filtered on later.
Write the filter as structure

The filter is data, not words in the query: product = motor AND region = MH AND doc_type = circular AND effective_from ≥ 1 April 2025. Embedding “motor circulars for Maharashtra” only nudges similarity; a filter enforces it.
Filter inside the search

query_filter goes with the query vector, so the engine checks the condition while it walks the graph and only matching chunks enter the top 10. hnsw_ef widens the candidate list when the filter is strict.
Let the planner use cardinality

The filter matches about 10,000 of 20,00,000 chunks, or 0.5%. For a set that small, Qdrant's planner reads the matching ids from the payload index and scores them exactly: 10,000 distances, 100% recall, a few milliseconds.
Never filter after a small top-k

The anti-pattern searches first and filters afterwards. With 0.5% of chunks matching, the global top 10 holds 10 × 0.005 = 0.05 matching chunks on average, so the list usually comes back empty. Measure recall per selectivity band, not only on unfiltered queries.

DDL = [
    "ALTER TABLE chunks ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY",                    #@1
    "ALTER TABLE chunks FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY",                     #@1
    """CREATE POLICY tenant_only ON chunks
       USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id'))""",        #@1
    "CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING gin (acl)",   # acl text[]: allowed groups  #@3
]

def search(user, query_vec, k=10):
    with psycopg.connect(APP_DSN) as conn:      # app role: not the owner  #@1
        register_vector(conn)
        with conn.transaction():
            conn.execute("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, true)",  #@2
                         (user.tenant_id,))     # from the verified token   #@2
            conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order")  #@4
            groups = [f"{user.tenant_id}:{g}" for g in user.groups]        #@3
            return conn.execute(
                """SELECT doc_id, body FROM chunks
                   WHERE acl && %s::text[]
                   ORDER BY embedding <=> %s LIMIT %s""",                  #@4
                (groups, query_vec, k)).fetchall()                         #@4

def on_acl_change(event):                # webhook from the source system  #@5
    with psycopg.connect(SYNC_DSN) as conn, conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, true)", (event.tenant_id,))
        conn.execute("UPDATE chunks SET acl = %s WHERE doc_id = %s",        #@5
                     ([f"{event.tenant_id}:{g}" for g in event.groups], event.doc_id))  #@5

def offboard(tenant_id):                 # contract ended: erase the client  #@6
    with psycopg.connect(ADMIN_DSN) as conn, conn.transaction():
        n = conn.execute("DELETE FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = %s",         #@6
                         (tenant_id,)).rowcount
        audit_log("tenant_erased", tenant_id=tenant_id, rows=n)             #@6
steps: Put the tenant rule in the database

LendStack keeps all 400 NBFC clients' chunks in one pgvector table, so a row-level security policy compares every row's tenant_id with the tenant set for the session. FORCE applies it to the table owner too, and the app connects as a separate role without BYPASSRLS. A query that forgets its WHERE clause still sees only one client.
Set the tenant from the token, per transaction

The tenant comes from the verified login token, never from the request body or the model. set_config(…, true) is local to the transaction, so when the pooled connection is reused for the next request it no longer carries t042. With no tenant set, the policy matches no rows or raises an error: it fails closed.
Store tenant-qualified ACLs

Each chunk carries the groups allowed to read it, copied from the source system. Priya is in pune-credit at t042, so her groups become t042:pune-credit. Another client also has a pune-credit group; without the prefix, an ACL check alone would let her match its chunks.
Check permission in the query

acl && groups sits in the WHERE clause, so only chunks Priya may read are ranked and the top 10 is full. The iterative scan keeps walking the HNSW index when the filter removes candidates. Forbidden text never reaches the prompt, so no instruction to the model is needed to hide it.
Sync ACL changes on events

When a branch manager removes someone in the source system, a webhook updates acl within about a minute. With a nightly sync the average stale window is 12 hours: 2,400 revocations a day × 0.05 queries an hour × 12 hours is about 1,440 exposures a day. Syncing on change brings that to about 2.
Erase a client on offboarding

When a client leaves, delete its chunks by tenant, then its caches, backups past their retention and any copies in evaluation sets, and record the erasure in an audit log. Under India's DPDP Act, personal data must be erased once its purpose is served. A namespace or shard per tenant makes this a single drop instead of a large delete.

from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models

client = QdrantClient(url="http://localhost:6333")
# 2 crore product vectors × 1,024 dims × 4 bytes ≈ 82 GB as float32        #@1
client.create_collection(
    "products",
    vectors_config=models.VectorParams(size=1024, distance=models.Distance.COSINE,
                                       on_disk=True),        # originals on SSD  #@3
    quantization_config=models.BinaryQuantization(                               #@2
        binary=models.BinaryQuantizationConfig(always_ram=True)),  # 128 B each  #@2
)

hits = client.query_points(
    "products", query=query_vec, limit=10,
    search_params=models.SearchParams(
        quantization=models.QuantizationSearchParams(
            rescore=True,            # re-rank with float32 from SSD               #@4
            oversampling=4.0)),      # 40 binary candidates for a top 10          #@5
).points
# recall@10 vs exact search: binary 74%, binary + rescore ×4 96%              #@6
steps: Size the problem
Bazaar Kart, a fictional marketplace, has 2 crore product vectors of 1,024 dims. As float32 that is 2 crore × 4,096 bytes = 81.9 GB of RAM, about ₹49,140 a month at ₹600 per GB-month.
Choose the encoding
int8 cuts it 4× to 20.5 GB. Binary keeps one bit per dimension: 128 bytes a vector, 2.6 GB in RAM. PQ with 64 one-byte codes would be 1.3 GB but needs training.
Keep the originals on SSD
The float32 vectors stay on disk. They are not searched; they are read only for the few candidates that need a precise score.
Rescore
The compressed index finds candidates with fast Hamming distance, then each candidate is re-ranked with its float32 vector.
Oversample
Fetching 4 × 10 = 40 candidates gives the rescoring step room to fix the order and recover near misses.
Measure recall
Against exact search on 1,000 real queries, binary alone finds 74% of the true top 10; with rescoring at ×4 it finds 96%, in 13 ms instead of 40 ms.

steps: Write the constraints down

Suvidha Finance, a fictional NBFC, has 1 crore chunks, expects 3× growth in two years, wants p95 under 50 ms, needs filters and hybrid search, and must keep vectors in its own cloud account. The team can spare about 20 operations hours a month.
Shortlist on hard constraints
A managed serverless store in the vendor’s account fails the residency rule, so it is out before any benchmark. pgvector, a self-hosted engine and the existing OpenSearch cluster remain.
Benchmark on your own data
Load a real sample with its metadata and replay 1,000 logged queries with their filters. Public benchmarks use other data and hardware.
Measure what you will pay for
Record recall at 10, p95 latency, monthly cost and operations hours for each finalist.
Decide
At 1 crore, pgvector’s p95 is 60 ms; a self-hosted Qdrant cluster gives 20 ms for ₹40,000 a month and about 16 operations hours. It meets every constraint.
Keep an exit
Export ids, vectors, metadata and ACLs nightly in an open format, so a later move is a reload, not a rewrite.

ivf.sc: A fintech keeps 2 million support-article chunks in Postgres. An IVFFlat index with 2,000 lists (rows ÷ 1,000) builds in minutes, and setting probes to about 45 (√lists) gives the recall they need, without adding a separate vector database.

lib: The Postgres extension for vectors. Supports IVFFlat and HNSW indexes alongside your normal tables and SQL.
code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  body      text,
  embedding vector(384)
);

-- Build AFTER loading data: clusters are learned from existing rows
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (lists = 2000);                  -- ≈ rows / 1000 for 2M rows

SET ivfflat.probes = 45;                -- ≈ √lists; raise for better recall

SELECT id, body
FROM chunks
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1               -- cosine distance to the query vector
LIMIT 5;

CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);   -- pgvector defaults

SET hnsw.ef_search = 80;                 -- default 40; higher = better recall

SELECT id, body
FROM chunks
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT 10;

import hnswlib

index = hnswlib.Index(space="cosine", dim=384)
index.init_index(max_elements=5_000_000, M=16, ef_construction=200)
index.add_items(vectors, ids)            # vectors: (n, 384) float32

index.set_ef(80)                         # query-time recall / latency dial
labels, distances = index.knn_query(query_vec, k=10)

from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models
client = QdrantClient("localhost", port=6333)

client.create_collection(
    "archive",
    vectors_config=models.VectorParams(size=1024, distance=models.Distance.COSINE),
    quantization_config=models.BinaryQuantization(
        binary=models.BinaryQuantizationConfig(always_ram=True)),   # layer 1 in RAM
)

hits = client.query_points(
    "archive", query=query_vec, limit=100,
    search_params=models.SearchParams(
        quantization=models.QuantizationSearchParams(
            rescore=True,          # layer 2: rescore with full vectors
            oversampling=10.0)),   # fetch 1,000 cheap candidates for 100 results
).points

top10 = cross_encoder_rerank(query_text, hits)[:10]           # layer 3

import psycopg
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

conn = psycopg.connect("dbname=suraksha", autocommit=True)
register_vector(conn)

conn.execute("""
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS chunks_emb_hnsw
    ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS chunks_meta_idx
    ON chunks (product, region, doc_type, effective_from);
""")

def embed(text):
    """Stub: return a numpy float32 vector from your embedding model."""
    raise NotImplementedError

def search(question, product, region, doc_type, since, k=10):
    qvec = embed(question)
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 100")
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order")
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.max_scan_tuples = 40000")
        return conn.execute("""
            SELECT id, title, embedding <=> %s AS distance
            FROM chunks
            WHERE product = %s AND region = %s
              AND doc_type = %s AND effective_from >= %s
            ORDER BY embedding <=> %s
            LIMIT %s""",
            (qvec, product, region, doc_type, since, qvec, k)).fetchall()

rows = search("own-damage claim rules after flooding", "motor", "MH",
              "circular", dt.date(2025, 4, 1))
for row in rows:
    print(row)

from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models

client = QdrantClient(url="http://localhost:6333")

client.create_collection(
    collection_name="loan_docs",
    vectors_config=models.VectorParams(size=768, distance=models.Distance.COSINE),
    hnsw_config=models.HnswConfigDiff(payload_m=16, m=0),   # a graph per tenant
)
client.create_payload_index(
    collection_name="loan_docs",
    field_name="tenant_id",
    field_schema=models.KeywordIndexParams(type=models.KeywordIndexType.KEYWORD,
                                           is_tenant=True),
)
client.create_payload_index(collection_name="loan_docs", field_name="acl",
                            field_schema=models.PayloadSchemaType.KEYWORD)

def search(token: str, question: str, k: int = 10):
    user = verify_token(token)                    # tenant comes from the token
    groups = [f"{user.tenant_id}:{g}" for g in user.groups]
    allowed = models.Filter(must=[
        models.FieldCondition(key="tenant_id",
                              match=models.MatchValue(value=user.tenant_id)),
        models.FieldCondition(key="acl", match=models.MatchAny(any=groups)),
    ])
    hits = client.query_points("loan_docs", query=embed(question),
                               query_filter=allowed, limit=k)
    return [p.payload["text"] for p in hits.points]

import numpy as np, faiss
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.quantization import quantize_embeddings

model = SentenceTransformer("mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-large-v1")
docs = [line.strip() for line in open("products.txt", encoding="utf-8")]
queries = [line.strip() for line in open("queries.txt", encoding="utf-8")]
d = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)
q = model.encode(queries, normalize_embeddings=True)

exact = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d.shape[1]); exact.add(d)
_, truth = exact.search(q, 10)

bits = quantize_embeddings(d, precision="ubinary")
binary = faiss.IndexBinaryFlat(d.shape[1]); binary.add(bits)
_, cand = binary.search(quantize_embeddings(q, precision="ubinary"), 40)

hits = 0
for i, c in enumerate(cand):
    top = c[np.argsort(-(d[c] @ q[i]))[:10]]      # rescore with float32
    hits += len(set(top) & set(truth[i]))
print("recall@10 after rescoring:", hits / (10 * len(queries)))
print("bytes per vector:", bits.shape[1], "vs", d.shape[1] * 4)
compress.note: The model name is an example; binary works best with models of 1,000 or more dimensions. The recall check compares against exact float32 search on the same queries.

import json, time, statistics, numpy as np, psycopg
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

conn = psycopg.connect("dbname=search", autocommit=True)
register_vector(conn)
queries = [json.loads(l) for l in open("queries_with_truth.jsonl")]   # vec, branch, truth_ids

lat, hits = [], 0
for q in queries:
    t = time.perf_counter()
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT id FROM chunks WHERE branch = %s ORDER BY embedding <=> %s LIMIT 10",
        (q["branch"], np.array(q["vec"]))).fetchall()
    lat.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
    hits += len({r[0] for r in rows} & set(q["truth_ids"]))

print("recall@10", round(hits / (10 * len(queries)), 3))
print("p95 ms", round(statistics.quantiles(lat, n=20)[18], 1))

ivf.title: Training an IVF index on claims data
ivf.code:
xb = np.load("claims.npy").astype("float32")   # 4,000,000 × 768, rows sorted by date
faiss.normalize_L2(xb)
nlist = 2000                                     # ≈ √rows above 1M rows
quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatIP(768)
index = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, 768, nlist, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
index.train(xb[:100_000])                        # train k-means on 100k vectors
index.add(xb)
ivf.explain: The rows are sorted by date, so the first 100,000 are the oldest claims only. k-means places all 2,000 centroids where the old data sits, newer kinds of claim pile into a few huge lists, and recall and speed both suffer. The sample size is fine, at 50 points per centroid; the problem is which rows they are. Train on a random sample drawn from the whole table.

also.3: √4,000,000 = 2,000, which matches pgvector’s rule of thumb above 1 million rows. This line is fine.

hnsw.title: An HNSW index for cosine search in pgvector
hnsw.explain: The index uses the L2 operator class, but the query orders by <=>, which is cosine distance. pgvector only uses an index whose operator class matches the operator in ORDER BY, so every query falls back to a full sequential scan. Build the index with vector_cosine_ops.
hnsw.fix: CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)

also.3: m = 16 and ef_construction = 64 are pgvector’s defaults. Nothing wrong here.
also.4: Raising ef_search above the default of 40 is the normal query-time recall dial.
also.6: <=> is cosine distance, which matches the comment. The index is what disagrees.

diskann.title: Sizing RAM for a DiskANN deployment
diskann.code:
def diskann_ram_gb(n, dims, pq_bytes, cache_gb=16):
    full_tb = n * dims * 4 / 1e12            # full-precision vectors, kept on SSD
    codes_gb = n * dims * pq_bytes / 1e9     # PQ codes held in RAM
    return codes_gb + cache_gb

print(diskann_ram_gb(1_000_000_000, 768, 32))
diskann.explain: A PQ code is pq_bytes per vector in total, not per dimension. Multiplying by dims inflates the estimate 768-fold, to about 24.6 TB instead of 32 GB of codes, and would wrongly rule DiskANN out.
diskann.fix: codes_gb = n * pq_bytes / 1e9            # PQ codes held in RAM

also.2: Full vectors are 4 bytes per float32 dimension: 1 billion × 768 × 4 B ≈ 3.1 TB. Correct, and they live on SSD.
also.4: Adding a fixed cache and working-memory allowance is a sensible part of the estimate.

las.title: A three-layer coarse-to-fine search
las.code:
bits = np.packbits(emb > 0, axis=1)                 # binary codes in RAM
ham = POP[bits ^ np.packbits(q > 0)].sum(axis=1)     # Hamming distance to all
c1 = np.argpartition(ham, 1000)[:1000]              # layer 1: 1,000 candidates
c2 = c1[np.argsort(ham[c1])[:100]]                  # layer 2: rescore to 100
c3 = c2[np.argsort(-(emb[c2] @ q))[:10]]            # layer 3: exact, top 10
las.explain: Layer 2 re-sorts the candidates by the same Hamming distance that chose them, so it adds no precision: it simply keeps the 100 best binary scores and throws away true neighbours that binary codes ranked slightly lower. The rescore must use a more precise representation, such as int8 or full vectors.
las.fix: c2 = c1[np.argsort(-(i8[c1].astype(np.int32) @ q8))[:100]]   # int8 rescore (i8, q8 as in the lesson)

also.1: Keeping the sign of each dimension is exactly how binary quantization works.
also.3: argpartition returns the 1,000 smallest distances in no particular order, which is all a candidate set needs.
also.5: The final exact rescore with full vectors is correct.

hybrid.title: Reciprocal rank fusion
hybrid.explain: RRF adds 1 ÷ (k + rank), not 1 ÷ (k × rank). With a product, k only rescales every score, so it no longer damps the top ranks: rank 1 is worth twice rank 2, and a document first in only one list ties with one that is second in both. With k + rank, 1/61 and 1/62 are close, so agreement between lists wins.

also.4: start=1 is correct: RRF ranks start at 1.
also.6: A higher fused score is better, so reverse=True is right.

metafilter.title: A filter that is built but never sent
metafilter.code:
def find_circulars(qvec, region, since):
    flt = models.Filter(must=[
        models.FieldCondition(key="region", match=models.MatchValue(value=region)),
        models.FieldCondition(key="effective_from", range=models.DatetimeRange(gte=since))])
    hits = client.query_points("suraksha_docs", query=qvec, limit=10).points
    return [h for h in hits
            if h.payload["region"] == region and h.payload["effective_from"] >= since]
metafilter.explain: The filter is built but never passed to the search, so the database returns the global top 10 and the list comprehension filters them afterwards. If 0.5% of chunks match, those 10 hold 10 × 0.005 = 0.05 matching chunks on average, so the handler usually gets an empty list. Pass the filter into the query so it is applied during the search.

also.3: Correct: an exact keyword match on the region field, which should have a keyword payload index.
also.4: Correct: a datetime range condition, backed by a datetime payload index.

tenancy.title: A permission filter without a tenant
tenancy.code:
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
from qdrant_client.models import Filter, FieldCondition, MatchAny, MatchValue
client = QdrantClient(url=QDRANT_URL)

def search(user, q_vec):
    allowed = Filter(must=[FieldCondition(key="acl", match=MatchAny(any=user.groups))])
    hits = client.query_points("chunks", query=q_vec, query_filter=allowed, limit=10)
    return [p.payload["text"] for p in hits.points]
tenancy.explain: The filter checks only the user’s groups, and group names such as "pune-credit" or "credit-ops" exist at many clients. A loan officer at one NBFC therefore matches chunks shared with the same group name at every other client. The tenant must be a separate condition taken from the verified token, and the groups should be prefixed with the tenant.
tenancy.fix: allowed = Filter(must=[FieldCondition(key="tenant_id", match=MatchValue(value=user.tenant_id)), FieldCondition(key="acl", match=MatchAny(any=[f"{user.tenant_id}:{g}" for g in user.groups]))])

also.7: Correct: the filter is passed to the search, so it is applied inside the index, not after ranking.
also.8: Correct: only the payloads of allowed points are returned.

compress.title: Rescoring binary candidates
compress.code:
bits_q = quantize_embeddings(q, precision="ubinary")
_, cand = binary_index.search(bits_q, 10)          # top 10 from binary codes
for i, c in enumerate(cand):
    top = c[np.argsort(-(full[c] @ q[i]))[:10]]    # rescore with float32
    results.append(top)
compress.explain: Rescoring can only reorder the candidates it is given. Fetching exactly 10 from the binary index means true neighbours missed by the coarse codes never get a chance.

also.1: Quantising the query the same way as the documents is right.
also.4: Rescoring with the float32 vectors is the correct step.

choosevs.title: Benchmarking two finalists
choosevs.code:
queries = load_real_queries("logs/search_sample.jsonl", n=1000)
for store in ["pgvector", "qdrant"]:
    db = connect(store)
    db.load("sample_20lakh.parquet")
    r = bench(db, queries, k=10, with_filters=False)
    print(store, r.recall_at_10, r.p95_ms)
choosevs.explain: Production search always filters by branch and product. Filtered search behaves very differently across stores, so a benchmark without filters can pick the wrong one.

also.1: Real logged queries are the right input.
also.4: Loading the same real sample into both stores is fair.

2: What does training learn?
The nlist centroids that define the lists
A graph of links between neighbouring vectors
k-means on a sample learns one centroid per list. Nothing is stored in the lists yet.
3: Where is each vector stored?
In every list whose centroid is within a set radius
In exactly one list: the one with its nearest centroid
Each vector joins the list of its closest centroid, so the lists partition the data.
4: How does the query choose which lists to scan?
It compares itself with every centroid and takes the nprobe closest
It scans lists in order until it has 10 results
Comparing with the centroids is cheap: 2,000 comparisons instead of 2 million.
5: nprobe = 45 of 2,000 lists of similar size. About what share of vectors gets an exact distance?
About 45%
About 2%
45 ÷ 2,000 ≈ 2.25% of the lists, and so of the vectors when lists are balanced.
6: Recall@10 is 0.88 against a 0.95 target and the data hasn’t changed. What do you try first?
Rebuild the index with more lists
Raise nprobe, which needs no rebuild
nprobe is set at query time. Rebuild only when the data has drifted from the centroids.

2: With M = 16, about what share of nodes also appear on layer 1?
About 1 in 16
About half
The random level uses 1 ÷ ln M as its scale, so each layer up keeps about 1 in M nodes.
3: Why do links on the sparse top layer end up long?
Long links are added deliberately after the build
Few nodes live there, so each node’s nearest neighbours are far apart
Linking to the nearest nodes on a sparse layer naturally produces long hops across the space.
4: The top-layer walk reaches a node with no closer neighbour. What happens next?
Search stops and returns that node
Search drops to the layer below and continues from that node
Each layer’s result becomes the entry point for the next, finer layer.
5: Why keep ef_search candidates on layer 0 instead of just one?
A purely greedy walk can stop at a local minimum and miss true neighbours
It reduces the memory the graph needs
A wider candidate list explores around the greedy path and recovers neighbours it would skip.
6: Recall is 0.91 at ef_search = 40. Which change needs no rebuild?
Raising M to 32
Raising ef_search to 80
ef_search is a query-time setting. M and ef_construction are fixed when the graph is built.

2: Why does the Vamana graph keep some long-range edges?
So a search crosses the space in few hops, which means few SSD reads
So the graph can be stored without any RAM
Every hop costs a disk read, so a graph with short paths is what makes SSD search fast.
3: What sits in RAM at search time?
Full vectors for the most-queried nodes only
Compressed PQ codes for every vector, plus a cache of hot nodes
The PQ codes guide the walk. Full vectors and neighbour lists stay on SSD.
4: Why cache the nodes around the fixed entry point?
Every search passes through them, so caching saves the first SSD reads
They are usually the best answers
All queries start at the same medoid, so the first few hops are shared and worth keeping in RAM.
5: With L = 100 and beam_width = 4, about how many SSD round trips does a query take?
About 100
About 25
⌈100 ÷ 4⌉ = 25 round trips, each issuing up to 4 reads in parallel.
6: Where do the full-precision vectors for the final re-rank come from?
A second round of SSD reads after the search
The sectors already read during the search
Each 4 KB sector holds the full vector next to the neighbour list, so exact distances cost no extra I/O.

2: Why keep as many as 1,000 candidates from the Hamming scan?
Anything dropped here can never be recovered by later layers
Binary scoring cannot return fewer than 1,000
Later layers only reorder what they receive, so layer 1 must be generous.
3: What does the int8 layer add over the binary scan?
It finds vectors the binary layer missed
It restores most of the precision lost by keeping only sign bits
int8 keeps 256 levels per dimension instead of 2, so its ranking is close to full precision.
4: How many float32 vectors does layer 3 fetch from SSD?
All one million
Only the 100 survivors
Only 100 × 4 KB is read, which keeps the SSD layer cheap.
5: What does the cross-encoder order the final 10 by?
Relevance, reading the query and each passage together
Vector distance again, at higher precision
A cross-encoder scores the pair jointly, which captures relevance a distance cannot.
6: Layers retain 0.97, 0.99 and 1.0 of the true top 10. What survives end to end?
0.99, set by the best layer
About 0.96, the product of the three

2: Why apply the tenant filter before ranking rather than after?
Every candidate is one the user may see, and the page stays full
It raises the BM25 scores of allowed pages
Filtering after ranking can leak or leave gaps; filtering first avoids both.
3: Which list ranks D1, the page that contains “809”, first?
Dense
BM25
BM25 rewards the rare exact term. Dense search puts D3 first because its meaning is close.
4: Dense scores are cosines near 0.8; BM25 scores are near 14. How does RRF combine them?
It adds the raw scores
It adds 1 ÷ (60 + rank) from each list
Only ranks are used, so the two scoring scales never have to be compared.
5: D1 is 2nd in dense and 1st in BM25. D5 is only in BM25, at rank 2. Which ranks higher after fusion?
D1
D5
6: Why evaluate code-style and meaning-style queries separately?
Each method fails on a different kind, so an average can hide a regression
Cross-encoders can only handle one kind
A change that helps paraphrases can quietly hurt codes, and the reverse.

2: A chunk is stored with region “Maharashtra”, but queries filter on “MH”. What happens?
The filter matches it anyway, because the words mean the same
The filter silently excludes it
Filters are exact conditions, not similarity. Normalise values at ingestion, or the chunk is never found.
3: Why use a DatetimeRange instead of writing “from April 2025” into the query text?
The range is enforced; words in the query only nudge similarity
The embedding model reads dates precisely
Embeddings blur dates and codes. A structured condition either matches or it does not.
4: The filter goes into query_points. When is it checked?
During the graph walk, so only matching chunks enter the top 10
After the top 10 are returned, in the client
Filtering inside the search fills all 10 slots with matching chunks.
5: About 10,000 of 20 lakh chunks match. Why can the planner skip the HNSW graph?
Scoring 10,000 vectors exactly is cheap and gives 100% recall
The graph cannot store metadata
At about 0.1 ms per 1,000 vectors, 10,000 exact distances take about 1 ms, and nothing is approximate.
6: 0.5% of chunks match the filter. How many matching chunks does an unfiltered top 10 hold on average?
About 5
About 0.05
10 × 0.005 = 0.05. Post-filtering a small top-k with a rare filter usually returns nothing.

2: Where should the tenant id for a search come from?
The verified login token, set per transaction
A tenant_id field in the request body
Anything in the request can be edited by the caller. The token is signed, and set_config(…, true) clears the tenant when the transaction ends.
3: Priya is in pune-credit at client t042. Another client also has a pune-credit group. What should her filter contain?
pune-credit
t042:pune-credit
Group names repeat across clients; prefixing them with the tenant keeps an ACL match inside one client.
4: Permission is checked in the query instead of after retrieval. What happens to the top 10?
It stays full, because only allowed chunks are ranked
It shrinks when forbidden chunks are removed
Filtering after ranking removes results and leaves short pages; filtering in the query ranks only what the user may see.
5: 2,400 revocations a day, 0.05 queries an hour per revoked document, nightly sync (12-hour average window). Roughly how many stale exposures a day?
2,400 × 0.05 × 12 = 1,440. An hourly sync would give 60, and syncing on change about 2.
6: A client leaves LendStack. What else must be erased besides its rows in the vector table?
Nothing: the rows are the data
Caches, backups past retention and copies in evaluation sets
Copies of the same text live in caches, backups and test sets; erasure is only complete when those are handled and logged.

2: Binary codes for 1,024 dims take how many bytes?
One bit per dimension: 1,024 ÷ 8 = 128 bytes.
3: Where do the float32 originals live?
On SSD, read only for candidates
In RAM next to the codes
Only a few dozen are read per query, so disk is fine.
4: What does rescoring change?
The order of candidates, using exact distances
Which vectors are in the index
It re-ranks what the compressed search found.
5: For a top 10 with oversampling 4, how many candidates are rescored?
6: Binary alone finds 74% of the true top 10. With rescoring ×4?
About 96%
Still 74%
Oversampling plus rescoring recovers most near misses.

2: Vectors must stay in the company’s own account. What happens to a store that runs only in the vendor’s account?
It is ruled out before benchmarking
It wins if it is fastest
Hard constraints come first.
3: Which queries should the benchmark use?
1,000 logged real queries with their filters
A public dataset
Your data and filters decide behaviour.
4: Besides recall and latency, what must be recorded?
Monthly cost and operations hours
Only the vendor’s claims
Staff time is part of cost.
5: pgvector p95 is 60 ms against a 50 ms target. Result?
It misses the target at this scale
It meets it
6: Why export vectors and metadata nightly?
So a later move is a reload, not a rewrite
To speed up queries
It keeps the choice reversible.

ivf: Vectors are grouped into clusters with k-means.
Each cluster is represented by its centroid.
probes: scanning only the nearest lists
A query scans only the few lists whose centroids are closest.
More probes raise recall and cost.
Centroids are learned from the data present when the index is built.
Rebuild when new data drifts away from the clusters.
hnsw: Vectors are nodes linked to their close neighbours.
layers: sparse on top, every vector at the bottom
Upper layers are sparse with long links; the bottom holds every vector.
Search enters at the top and hops towards the query, dropping a layer at a time.
ef_search sets the candidate list at query time.
M and ef_construction at build time
M and ef_construction are fixed when the graph is built.
Vectors and links must sit in RAM, and strict filters can hurt recall.
diskann: The index and full vectors live on SSD.
Only compressed PQ codes are kept in RAM.
the Vamana graph and few hops
A single-layer graph with long-range edges needs few hops.
few SSD reads per query or beam search
Each query reads only a handful of SSD pages, several at a time.
Full vectors read along the way give exact final distances.
It serves billions of vectors with modest RAM.
las: The first layer uses cheap compressed vectors over everything.
Each layer sees far fewer items than the last.
Later layers are precise and costly per item.
What the first layer drops can never come back.
measuring recall and latency per layer
Measure recall and latency after each layer.
hybrid: dense or vector search for meaning
Dense search finds matches by meaning.
sparse or keyword search for exact terms
BM25 finds exact terms and codes.
The two result lists are fused.
Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1 ÷ (k + rank) and ignores raw scores.
Raw scores sit on different scales; normalize or use ranks.
Apply permission and tenant filters in the database.
metafilter: Each chunk carries structured fields such as date, product, region and version.
a filter combined with vector search
The query combines similarity with a hard condition on those fields.
where the filter runs: pre, post or inside
The filter can run before, after or during the vector search.
post-filtering loses results when filters are rare
Post-filtering a small top-k leaves k × selectivity matches on average.
selectivity or cardinality decides the strategy
How many items match decides between an exact scan and filtered ANN.
index the fields you filter on
Payload or attribute indexes make filters fast and let the planner estimate matches.
tenancy: Each customer’s data is kept apart from every other customer’s.
Isolation uses a namespace or shard per tenant, or a database policy such as row-level security.
The tenant comes from the verified login, not from the request or the model.
document ACLs filtered in the query
Document permissions are filtered inside the query, before ranking.
The model is never asked to hide forbidden text; it never receives it.
sync on change and erase on offboarding
ACL changes sync quickly, and a departing tenant’s data is erased.
compress: The index fits in far less RAM.
choosevs: Size now and in two years.
Benchmark finalists on your own queries.

ivf: A bank’s complaint-search table in pgvector holds 800,000 rows. What value of lists does pgvector suggest for an IVFFlat index?
Up to 1 million rows, pgvector suggests lists ≈ rows ÷ 1,000: 800,000 ÷ 1,000 = 800.
A brokerage embeds 16 million research-note chunks in pgvector. What value of lists is suggested?
Above 1 million rows the suggestion is √rows, and √16,000,000 = 4,000.
An IVFFlat product index had 0.96 recall at launch and now has 0.82. Which of these could explain the drop? Select all that apply.
Whole new product categories were added after the index was built
The index was built when the table held 5% of today’s rows
Many queries now fall near cluster borders
Stale centroids, unrepresentative training data and border queries all cost recall. Raising probes improves recall.
An IVF index over policy clauses has 2,500 lists. What starting value for probes does pgvector suggest?
Start probes around √lists: √2,500 = 50, then tune against measured recall.
3 million merchant-description vectors sit in 3,000 lists of roughly equal size. With probes = 30, about how many vectors get exact distances per query?
Each list holds about 3,000,000 ÷ 3,000 = 1,000 vectors, and 30 lists × 1,000 = 30,000, or 1% of the data.
A hospital created an IVFFlat index on an empty table, then loaded 1.2 million note embeddings. Recall is very poor. What fixes it?
Rebuild the index now that representative data is loaded
Switch from cosine to L2 distance
Load more rows into the same index
IVF learns its centroids when the index is built. Built on no data, the clusters are meaningless until it is rebuilt.
The index has a single graph layer
Vectors inside each list are stored uncompressed, so distances within a list are exact
Every list has exactly the same size
The centroids are fixed and never trained
Flat means raw vectors in the lists. IVF-PQ is the variant that compresses them.
Which of these can be changed per query without rebuilding the index? Select all that apply.
probes, nprobe and ef_search are query-time settings. The number of lists is fixed when the index is trained.
A shipment-search index has recall@10 of 0.86 at probes = 10 against a 0.95 target, with latency to spare. What do you try first?
Rebuild with twice as many lists
Drop the index and use exact search
probes is the query-time recall dial. Rebuild only if the data has drifted from the centroids.
A developer sets probes equal to lists. What does the search become?
An exact scan of every vector, plus the centroid comparisons
A search over half the lists
A rebuild of the index at query time
Scanning every list means computing every distance, which is exact search with extra overhead.
A FAISS IVF index uses nlist = 4,096. FAISS warns when there are fewer than 39 training points per centroid. About how many training vectors do you need at minimum?
A bank builds an IVF index over 10 million transaction-narration embeddings. Which steps are sound? Select all that apply.
Train on a random sample rather than the first rows loaded
Build the index before loading any data, so inserts are fast
Centroids must be learned from representative data, and √rows is the suggested list count above 1 million rows.
A law firm stores 768-dimension float32 vectors in IVF-PQ with 64-byte codes. What is the compression factor inside the lists?
After a build on early data, the largest of 16 lists holds 40% of all vectors. A query that probes 2 lists including that one scans at least what share?
That one list alone holds 40% of the rows. Skewed lists make probing expensive, which is why you rebuild on representative data.
Why do queries near a cluster border need more probes?
Their true neighbours can sit in a neighbouring list that is not among the nearest centroids
The distance metric changes near borders
Choosing lists by centroid distance can skip the list that holds a neighbour just across the border.
When is IVFFlat a reasonable choice over HNSW? Select all that apply.
Fast index builds matter on a moderate dataset
Data is batch-loaded and the index is rebuilt nightly
Memory is tight and slightly lower recall is acceptable
Data arrives continuously and drifts, with no chance to rebuild
IVF builds quickly and uses little memory, but it depends on trained centroids, so drifting data favours HNSW.
2 million vectors sit in 2,000 balanced lists and probes = 45. About how many vectors are scanned per query?
Each list holds about 1,000 vectors, so 45 lists × 1,000 = 45,000, which is 45 ÷ 2,000 = 2.25%.
A pgvector query filters to one circle (5% of rows) and uses IVFFlat with probes = 10. It returns 3 rows instead of 10. Why?
IVFFlat cannot be combined with a WHERE clause
The filter is applied after the probed lists are scanned, so few candidates match
Only about 5% of the scanned candidates survive the filter. Raise probes, or use iterative index scans in pgvector 0.8 and later.
What should you monitor after deploying an IVF index? Select all that apply.
Recall@10 against exact search on sample queries
The largest list’s share of rows
Recall, list balance and latency show when probes need tuning or the index needs rebuilding.
A learning platform on Postgres has 1.2 million lesson chunks and wants semantic search without running a new database. What fits?
pgvector with an IVFFlat or HNSW index
pgvector adds vector indexes next to existing tables and SQL filters, with no new system to run.
hnsw: An HNSW index gives recall@10 of 0.89 against a 0.95 target, and latency has headroom. What do you change first?
ef_search is the query-time dial and needs no rebuild.
A bank indexes 10 million 768-dimension float32 vectors with HNSW. How much RAM do the raw vectors need?
768 × 4 B = 3,072 B per vector, and 3,072 B × 10 million ≈ 30.7 GB.
The same 10 million vectors use M = 16, so the bottom layer keeps up to 32 links per node at 4 bytes each. How much memory do those links add?
32 × 4 B = 128 B per node, and 128 B × 10 million = 1.28 GB.
Which of these changes require rebuilding a pgvector HNSW index? Select all that apply.
m, ef_construction and the operator class are fixed at build time. ef_search is set per query or session.
With M = 16, about what share of nodes reaches layer 2?
Each layer up keeps about 1 in M nodes, so layer 2 has about 1 in 16 × 16 = 256.
What are pgvector’s default HNSW settings?
pgvector defaults to m = 16, ef_construction = 64 and hnsw.ef_search = 40.
Call-transcript embeddings arrive all day, and the topics shift from month to month. Why does HNSW suit this better than IVF?
It needs no training step; new vectors are linked in as they arrive
IVF depends on centroids learned at build time. HNSW inserts need no training, so drift does not stale the index.
A claims search filters to one branch (0.5% of rows) after the HNSW search, and returns 2 results instead of 10. What is the best fix?
Filter-aware search or iterative scans, or partitioning by branch
Post-filtering throws away almost every candidate. Filter during the search, scan iteratively, or partition by the filter.
Which of these increase the memory an HNSW index needs? Select all that apply.
Links grow with M and node count, and vectors grow with dimensions. ef_search only affects per-query work.
Which of these are known weaknesses of HNSW? Select all that apply.
Vectors and links must sit in RAM
Heavy deletes and updates degrade the graph
It needs k-means training before use
Memory, graph decay under churn and filtered search are the classic problems. HNSW has no training step.
An HNSW search over 5 million fare-rule vectors compares about 3,000 vectors per query. What share of the index is that?
Measurements: ef_search 40 gives recall 0.91 at 2.1 ms; 80 gives 0.96 at 3.4 ms; 160 gives 0.98 at 6.2 ms. The target is recall ≥ 0.95 with p95 under 5 ms. Which setting?
Only ef_search = 80 meets both the recall and the latency target.
Which practices make an HNSW benchmark trustworthy before launch? Select all that apply.
Measure recall against exact search on real queries
Measure p95 latency under concurrent load
Test on random vectors from a different dataset
Real queries, real filters and realistic load reflect production. Random vectors hide how your data clusters.
What happens when ef_construction is raised from 64 to 200?
A better-connected graph and a slower build
Faster queries at the same ef_search, with no other cost
A wider build-time search finds better neighbours for each insert, at the cost of build time.
A legal archive holds 2 million 1,536-dimension float32 vectors in HNSW with M = 16 (32 bottom-layer links of 4 B each). About how much RAM do vectors plus links need?
Vectors: 2 million × 6,144 B ≈ 12.29 GB. Links: 2 million × 128 B ≈ 0.26 GB. Total ≈ 12.5 GB.
Which pgvector pairing lets an HNSW index serve a cosine-distance query?
Any operator class works with any operator
The index operator class must match the ORDER BY operator: <=> is cosine distance and needs vector_cosine_ops.
A fraud team studies how an HNSW query runs. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
The search enters at the top layer
It moves greedily to closer neighbours
It drops a layer when no neighbour is closer
It scans every vector on layer 0
The bottom layer is explored with an ef_search-sized candidate list, not scanned in full.
An insurer has 400 million 768-dimension vectors (about 1.23 TB) and a server with 512 GB of RAM. What approach fits?
DiskANN, or heavy quantization, rather than full vectors in RAM
IVFFlat with all vectors in RAM
400 million × 3,072 B ≈ 1.23 TB will not fit in 512 GB, so the full vectors must leave RAM or be compressed.
With M = 4, a graph needs a much larger ef_search to reach the same recall. Why?
Each node has few links, so greedy walks get stuck more easily
Vectors are stored at lower precision
ef_search is ignored when M is small
The graph uses a different distance metric
A poorly connected graph offers fewer routes to the query, so the search has to explore more candidates.
A Python service holds 2 million vectors in process and needs HNSW without a database. Which tool fits?
hnswlib is a fast in-process HNSW library for Python and C++.
diskann: An ads platform has 1 billion 768-dimension float32 vectors. How much space do the full vectors take?
A marketplace stores 800 million listings as 32-byte PQ codes in RAM for DiskANN. How much RAM do the codes need?
Which of these make DiskANN query latency worse? Select all that apply.
Network block storage instead of local NVMe
A beam width of 1 with a long candidate list
A warm cache of nodes near the entry point
Heavy concurrent load saturating the SSD
Slow reads, many sequential round trips and SSD queueing all add latency. A warm cache saves reads.
A DiskANN search uses a candidate list L = 120 and a beam width of 4. About how many SSD round trips does a query take?
⌈120 ÷ 4⌉ = 30 round trips, each issuing up to 4 reads.
A radiology group has 20 million 512-dimension vectors (about 41 GB) on a server with 128 GB of RAM. Which index fits best?
20 million × 2,048 B ≈ 41 GB fits in RAM with room for links, and in-memory HNSW is faster than SSD reads.
Why does DiskANN store each node’s full vector in the same SSD sector as its neighbour list?
One read gives both the next hops and the exact distance for the final re-rank
It frees the SSD for other data
The walk needs the neighbour list anyway, so the full vector comes free for exact re-ranking.
During a DiskANN search, what decides which nodes to read next?
Exact distances from full vectors held in RAM
Approximate distances from the PQ codes held in RAM
Compressed codes in RAM guide the walk. Full vectors are read from SSD only for the visited nodes.
Each DiskANN node stores its 1,536-dimension float32 vector plus 64 neighbour IDs of 4 bytes and a 4-byte count. How many 4 KB sectors does a node need?
Which of these are DiskANN-based options? Select all that apply.
pgvectorscale, Milvus and FreshDiskANN all build on DiskANN. hnswlib implements HNSW.
A DiskANN index has recall 0.92 against a 0.95 target, with latency to spare. What do you change?
Raise the candidate list size L
A longer candidate list explores more of the graph and raises recall, at the cost of more reads.
A shop has 1 million product vectors and RAM to spare. How does DiskANN compare with in-memory HNSW here?
In-memory HNSW is usually faster, because nothing waits on SSD reads
DiskANN pays off when data exceeds RAM. At small scale, SSD reads only add latency.
PQ code size is raised from 32 to 64 bytes. Which of these happen? Select all that apply.
Recall improves at the same candidate list size
Distances that guide the walk become more accurate
Finer codes guide the search better and double RAM. The full vectors on SSD are unchanged.
Why benchmark DiskANN p95 latency under concurrent load rather than one query at a time?
SSD queues build up under concurrency, so single-query tests understate real latency
Many queries share the same device, and queueing on random reads shows up only under load.
A bank has 2 billion 768-dimension vectors and 256 GB of RAM. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
The full vectors take about 6.1 TB
32-byte PQ codes take 64 GB of RAM
In-memory HNSW would fit in 256 GB
128-byte codes alone would take all 256 GB
2 billion × 3,072 B ≈ 6.1 TB; × 32 B = 64 GB; × 128 B = 256 GB. Full vectors cannot fit in RAM.
With L = 100, raising the beam width from 4 to 8 changes the round trips from 25 to about how many?
⌈100 ÷ 8⌉ = ⌈12.5⌉ = 13 round trips, with more reads per trip.
An archive plans to index 3 billion documents with DiskANN. What should the plan account for?
Builds at this scale take many hours and a lot of memory, so schedule rebuilds
The index is rebuilt per query
Very large graph builds are slow and memory-hungry, which matters for rebuild schedules.
Listings change thousands of times an hour in a DiskANN-backed search. What should you use?
A static DiskANN index rebuilt after every insert
A streaming variant such as FreshDiskANN, or StreamingDiskANN in pgvectorscale
Streaming variants accept inserts and deletes without full rebuilds.
An airline stores 500 million vectors as 64-byte PQ codes and reserves 16 GB for cache and working memory. How much RAM does DiskANN need?
500 million × 64 B = 32 GB of codes, plus 16 GB = 48 GB.
Which conditions matter for good DiskANN performance? Select all that apply.
Local NVMe SSDs with fast random reads
Enough RAM for the PQ codes
A tuned candidate list and beam width
All full vectors held in RAM
DiskANN is designed so that full vectors stay on SSD. Fast disks, RAM for codes and tuning matter.
A payments firm on Postgres has 150 million vectors and wants to stay in Postgres. Which tool fits?
