pgvectorscale adds a DiskANN-style index to Postgres for datasets beyond comfortable RAM.
las: Layers keep 0.95, 0.99 and 1.0 of the true top 10. What is the end-to-end recall?
How many bytes does a binary code take for a 1,024-dimension vector?
Which statements about layered search are correct? Select all that apply.
Candidates dropped by the first layer are lost for good
Each later layer is more precise per item
The final layer scans the whole corpus
Coarse to fine: cheap and wide first, precise and narrow last. The final layer sees only a handful of items.
10 million 1,024-dimension vectors are stored as int8 for a rescoring layer. How much RAM does that take?
int8 is one byte per dimension: 10 million × 1,024 B ≈ 10.2 GB.
A news archive’s end-to-end recall is 0.80, while each later layer keeps almost everything it receives. What fixes it?
Keeping more candidates in the first layer
Later layers cannot recover what layer 1 dropped, so layer 1 needs a larger candidate set.
A Qdrant query asks for limit = 100 with oversampling = 4.0 and rescoring on. How many candidates are fetched from the quantized index?
Oversampling multiplies the limit: 100 × 4 = 400 candidates are rescored with full vectors to return 100.

Layer 1 costs 3 ms plus 0.004 ms per candidate and keeps 2,000. Layer 2 rescores those at 0.003 ms each and keeps 100. Layer 3 fetches the 100 at 0.05 ms each. A cross-encoder takes 1.2 ms per pair for 10 pairs. Total latency?
Which layer designs are reasonable for 50 million support chunks? Select all that apply.
Binary codes in RAM for layer 1
int8 rescoring of a few thousand candidates
Fetching full vectors from SSD only for the last hundred
Running the cross-encoder over all 50 million chunks
Each layer is sized to what it can afford. A cross-encoder over the whole corpus would take hours.
Why add an int8 layer between the binary scan and the float32 rescore? Select all that apply.
It avoids fetching thousands of float32 vectors from SSD
It restores most of the precision lost by binary codes
It recovers neighbours the binary layer dropped
int8 narrows the set cheaply and accurately in RAM. It can only reorder what layer 1 kept.
A cross-encoder costs 1.2 ms per pair and re-ranks 50 passages, pushing a 50 ms budget over. What is the most direct fix?
Re-rank fewer passages, such as 20, which takes 24 ms
50 × 1.2 = 60 ms breaks the budget; 20 × 1.2 = 24 ms fits.
A vendor says its product does “layered approximate search”. What should you understand by that?
A pattern rather than one standard algorithm: products call it phased ranking or rescoring, so check what it does
The name means different things in different products. Ask which layers it runs and how many candidates each keeps.
Which product expresses layered ranking as first-phase, second-phase and global-phase?
Vespa’s phased ranking runs a cheap first phase over many hits and costlier phases over fewer.
Binary quantization replaces 32-bit floats with 1 bit per dimension. What is the compression factor?
Which measurements do you need to size each layer? Select all that apply.
Layer 1 recall at several candidate counts
Sizing is empirical: measure what each layer keeps and costs, and check the whole pipeline.
Layer 1 keeps 0.90 of the true top 10. Every later layer keeps everything and a cross-encoder orders the result. What is the best possible vector recall@10?
It depends only on the cross-encoder
Later layers only reorder what layer 1 kept, so recall is capped at 0.90.
How much RAM do binary codes need for 200 million 1,024-dimension vectors?
1,024 bits = 128 B per vector, and 200 million × 128 B = 25.6 GB.
Which FAISS index rescores results from a quantized index with full vectors?
IndexRefineFlat wraps a compressed index and re-ranks its candidates with exact distances.
Which of these make the first layer miss true neighbours? Select all that apply.
Binary codes that lose too much information for this embedding model
A narrow or lossy first layer drops neighbours. The final re-ranker cannot cause first-layer misses.
Layer 1 keeps 0.98 of true neighbours at 1,000 candidates and 0.995 at 3,000, which adds 8 ms. The pipeline has 10 ms to spare. What do you choose?
The extra recall is permanent and fits the spare budget, since 8 ms is below 10 ms.
Where must full-precision vectors live for the final rescore?
Somewhere retrievable, such as on SSD; they need not be in RAM
Only the few final candidates need full vectors, so they can be fetched from disk.
hybrid: Dense search ranks a runbook 1st and BM25 ranks it 4th. With k = 60, what is its RRF score?
Shoppers type “running shoe size 9 model 41”. Why does hybrid search help?
The query mixes intent with exact size and model tokens
The query is too long for embeddings
Dense search captures “running shoe”; BM25 matches “9” and “41” exactly.
Which are valid ways to combine dense and BM25 results? Select all that apply.
Normalise each score list, then weight with α
Add raw BM25 and cosine scores directly
Keep only the list whose top score is higher
Ranks or normalised scores are comparable. Raw BM25 and cosine scores sit on different scales.
What does raising the RRF constant k from 10 to 60 do?
Reduces the advantage of top ranks, so agreement across lists matters more
With k = 10, rank 1 beats rank 2 by 1/11 versus 1/12; with k = 60 the gap between 1/61 and 1/62 is much smaller.
A multi-hospital search must never show one hospital’s notes to another. Where should the tenant filter go?
In the prompt, asking the LLM to ignore other hospitals
Inside the database, in both retrievers, before results leave it
Permissions belong in the database query itself, never in the LLM or after ranking.
Document A is 1st in dense and absent from BM25. Document B is 3rd in dense and 2nd in BM25. With k = 60, which ranks higher?
Clients search for the ISIN “INE002A01018” and dense search returns unrelated funds. What is the fix?
Add BM25 and fuse the results
An ISIN is a rare exact token. Keyword search matches it; embeddings blur it.
Which are real pitfalls of hybrid search? Select all that apply.
Two indexes to keep in sync
Raw scores are not comparable across methods
Filtering after ranking can leave too few results
RRF needs no training; it only uses ranks.
After min–max normalisation a product has dense 0.8 and sparse 0.2. With α = 0.7 on dense, what is its fused score?
Filtering after fusion leaves 3 of 5 results on the page. Which fixes work? Select all that apply.
Oversample before filtering, for example fetch 50 and then filter
Use the vector database’s filter-aware search
Filtering first, or fetching enough extra candidates, keeps the page full. k does not change how many results survive.
In a Weaviate hybrid query, what does alpha = 0 mean?
In Weaviate, alpha = 1 is pure vector search and alpha = 0 is pure keyword search.
What is the default rank constant for reciprocal rank fusion in Elasticsearch?
Elasticsearch’s rank_constant defaults to 60, the value used in the original RRF paper.
How should you evaluate a hybrid search change? Select all that apply.
Use separate code-style and meaning-style query sets
Compare recall@k for dense, sparse and fused
Check that permission filters leave no leaks
Look only at the average cosine similarity of top results
Each method fails on different queries, and permissions must be tested too. Cosine averages say nothing about fused quality.
Travellers search for flight numbers such as “AI 302”. Which part of a hybrid system handles them best?
Exact identifiers are a sparse-retrieval strength.
Each retriever returns only its top 5 before fusion. What is the risk?
A document ranked 8th in both lists is never fused, although agreement would lift it
At rank 8 in both, RRF gives 2 ÷ 68 ≈ 0.029, more than a rank-1 hit in one list (≈ 0.016). Retrieve 50–100 from each.
Why does hybrid search often beat either method alone?
It doubles the number of vectors
Dense and sparse fail on different queries, so fusion combines their strengths
Dense handles paraphrases, sparse handles exact terms, and fusion keeps both.
Three retrievers rank a document 1st, 2nd and 3rd. With k = 60, what is its RRF score?
Where can tenant filters go safely in a hybrid pipeline? Select all that apply.
As a pre-filter inside the vector search
As a filter inside the keyword query
Applied by the LLM when it writes the answer
In both retrievers, using the same tenant metadata
Both retrievers must filter inside the database. The LLM is not an access-control layer.
A Postgres team wants hybrid search without adding a new database. What fits?
pgvector plus Postgres full-text search, fused with RRF in SQL
pgvector handles vectors and Postgres full-text search handles keywords; RRF is a few lines of SQL.
Weighted fusion works well on one query set and badly on another. Why?
RRF would need an α too
The best α depends on the query mix, so tune it on a representative evaluation set
Code-heavy queries want more sparse weight and paraphrases want more dense weight.
metafilter: An insurer’s search takes the ANN top 10 and then keeps only motor circulars for Maharashtra, which are 0.5% of chunks. On average, how many results survive?
Expected survivors = k × selectivity = 10 × 0.005 = 0.05, so the list is usually empty.
A marketplace post-filters by “in stock in Pune”, which matches 4% of products. How many candidates must the ANN search fetch so that about 10 survive on average?
10 ÷ 0.04 = 250 candidates. The rarer the filter, the more oversampling post-filtering needs.
A bank’s RBI circular search filters on department = “Payments”, which matches 30% of 5 lakh chunks. Which strategy is usually the poorest fit?
Filtered ANN with a payload index
Pre-filtering with an exact scan of every matching chunk
30% of 5 lakh is 1,50,000 vectors to score exactly on every query. Broad filters suit filtered ANN or modest oversampling.
A filter matches 8,000 of 20 lakh chunks. Qdrant has a payload index on every filtered field. What is its planner likely to do?
Walk the HNSW graph and hope enough nodes match
Read the matching ids from the payload index and score them exactly
Return an error for low cardinality
For a small matching set, an exact scan is cheap and gives 100% recall; the payload index supplies the cardinality estimate.
A UPI dispute knowledge base stores the state as “MH” on some chunks and “Maharashtra” on others. Queries filter on “MH”. What happens?
Both match, because they mean the same thing
The query fails with an error
Filters are exact conditions. Normalise metadata values at ingestion.
A hospital’s guideline search should use only the current version of each protocol. What is the most reliable way?
Add “use the latest version” to the prompt
Store version or is_current as metadata and filter on it in the vector query
Embed the version number into the text
A structured filter guarantees the condition; prompt text and embeddings only encourage it.
Which are good candidates for metadata filters in a policy-wording search? Select all that apply.
Product line, such as motor or health
Filters work on hard, structured facts. Tone is fuzzy and belongs to ranking, not filtering.
With pgvector 0.8, a filtered HNSW query returns only 3 rows for LIMIT 10. Which setting keeps scanning the index until enough rows pass the WHERE clause?
Iterative index scans (strict_order or relaxed_order) continue the scan until enough filtered rows are found, up to max_scan_tuples.
Why should Qdrant payload indexes be created before a large bulk upload rather than after?
The HNSW graph can then be built with extra links that keep filtered searches connected
Qdrant builds filter-aware links when payload indexes exist at indexing time; adding them later misses that benefit until reindexing.
A SEBI-circular assistant embeds the query “circulars from 2025 on margin”. Results include 2019 circulars. What is missing?
A structured date filter instead of relying on the words “from 2025”
Embeddings blur dates. A range filter on the issue date enforces it.
Which signs suggest post-filtering is hurting recall? Select all that apply.
Rare filters return fewer than k results
Recall is fine on unfiltered queries but poor on filtered ones
Latency rises steadily with collection size for all queries
Raising the candidate count fills the empty slots
Short lists on rare filters, a gap between filtered and unfiltered recall, and relief from oversampling all point to post-filtering.
Suraksha General pre-filters exactly. Scoring costs about 0.1 ms per 1,000 vectors. A filter matches 50% of 20 lakh chunks. About how long does the scan take?
10,00,000 vectors × 0.1 ms per 1,000 = 100 ms. Broad filters make exact pre-filtering slow.

A citizen-services search must show only schemes for the user’s state and must never mix in other departments’ internal notes. Which part belongs to metadata filtering, and which to a separate control?
State is a relevance filter; blocking internal notes is access control and needs its own enforcement
State needs access control; internal notes need a re-ranker
Relevance filters narrow results; permissions and tenancy are a security boundary with their own design and tests.
A Weaviate collection has a very restrictive filter and filtered HNSW recall drops. Which strategy targets this case?
ACORN, which explores two-hop neighbours when direct ones are filtered out
ACORN keeps the graph walk connected when most neighbours fail the filter.
A search filters on merchant_category with 12 possible values but has no index on that field. What is the likely effect?
Each query checks the field on far more records than needed, adding latency and hurting planning
Unindexed filter fields force slow checks and prevent the engine from estimating cardinality.
A clinical-note search post-filters by ward. Which fixes restore a full top 10 for rare wards? Select all that apply.
Pass the filter into the vector query
Pre-filter and score the matching notes exactly when there are few
Filter inside the search, oversample enough, or scan the small matching set exactly. A smaller k just hides the problem.
An NBFC filters loan-policy chunks by product and version. Recall is 98% on broad filters and 40% on rare ones. What should the evaluation report?
Recall and latency per selectivity band: broad, medium and rare
Filter strategies fail differently by selectivity, so an average hides the rare-filter collapse.
A filter matches 5% of chunks. Post-filtering fetches 40 candidates. How many results survive on average?
Which statement about Pinecone metadata filters is accurate?
They are applied during the vector query, so results match the filter
They are applied only after results reach your application
They work only on vector values
They require a separate SQL database
Pinecone applies metadata filters inside the query using operators such as $eq, $in and $gte.
A bank moves from post-filtering to filtered ANN with payload indexes. What else should the team do? Select all that apply.
Remove the date field to save memory
Check that every filtered field has an index
Clean values, indexed fields and per-band measurement make filtered search trustworthy.
tenancy: A loan-servicing SaaS keeps 400 NBFC clients in one vector index and adds "tenant_id = X" in each search endpoint. A new “similar loans” endpoint ships without it. What is the design flaw?
Tenant isolation depends on every endpoint remembering a filter in app code
There are too many tenants for one index
Enforce the tenant below the app, with row-level security, a namespace per tenant or a single shared retrieval function, so one forgotten filter cannot leak.
A bank’s assistant is told in its system prompt: “Only use documents the user is allowed to see.” All retrieved chunks, allowed or not, go into the context. What is the risk?
None, if the model is large enough
Prompt injection or a clever question can extract forbidden text already in the context
A prompt instruction is not a permission check. Filter forbidden chunks out in the query so they never reach the model.
Where should a multi-tenant search take the tenant id from?
A tenant_id field in the JSON request body
The verified login token, set by the server for this request
The model’s guess from the question
A browser cookie the client can edit
Only the signed, verified token is trustworthy. Anything in the request can be changed by the caller.
A loan officer at client t042 is in the group "pune-credit". Another client also has a "pune-credit" group. The search filters only on groups. What happens?
She can retrieve the other client’s chunks shared with its pune-credit group
The other client’s officers lose access
Group names repeat across tenants. Filter on the tenant separately and prefix groups with it, for example t042:pune-credit.

An HR platform’s clients revoke 2,400 user–document permissions a day. A revoked user queries each lost document 0.05 times an hour. With an hourly ACL sync (average stale window 0.5 hours), how many stale exposures happen a day?
2,400 × 0.05 × 0.5 = 60 a day. A nightly sync (12-hour average) would give 1,440.
A hospital network’s search fetches the top 10 chunks, then removes those the doctor may not see. Often only 3 remain. What is the better design?
Ask the model to fill the gaps
Apply the permission filter inside the query so only allowed chunks are ranked
Turn off permissions for senior doctors
Filtering after ranking leaves short pages. Filtering in the query ranks only allowed chunks and keeps the page full.
Only 20% of a payments firm’s chunks are allowed for a typical support agent. If permissions are checked after retrieval, how many candidates must be fetched, on average, to end with 10 allowed ones?
10 ÷ 0.2 = 50 candidates on average, and more for a safety margin. Filtering in the query avoids the oversampling.
Which are ways to isolate tenants in a vector store? Select all that apply.
A system-prompt line naming the tenant
A Weaviate collection with multi-tenancy enabled, one tenant shard per client
Namespaces, database policies and tenant shards enforce isolation in the data layer. A prompt line enforces nothing.
A telecom SaaS uses Postgres row-level security and pooled connections. It sets the tenant with set_config('app.tenant_id', …, false). What can go wrong?
The setting persists on the pooled connection, so the next request may run as the previous tenant
The policy is ignored for SELECT
With false the setting lasts for the whole session. Use true, which is local to the transaction, and set it on every request.
A marketplace SaaS has 5,000 small sellers, each with a few thousand chunks. Which Qdrant setup fits?
One collection with a tenant_id payload index marked is_tenant
One collection with no tenant field
A separate Qdrant server per seller
Thousands of tiny tenants fit one collection with an is_tenant index, which stores each tenant’s vectors together; per-tenant collections add heavy overhead.
A departing NBFC client asks LendStack to erase its data. Which isolation model makes this simplest?
A shared index with a tenant filter
A namespace per tenant, deleted in one call
Keeping the data but hiding it in the prompt
Re-embedding the data with a new model
Deleting a namespace or tenant shard removes the whole client at once. A shared index needs a large delete by filter and a check that nothing is left.
A client leaves and its data must be erased once the purpose is served, as India’s DPDP Act expects. What should the erasure cover? Select all that apply.
Its chunks and vectors in the store
Copies in evaluation or test sets
Other clients’ chunks that mention the same RBI circular
Copies of the client’s text live in caches and test sets as well as the store. Other clients’ data is theirs and stays.
One big tenant bulk re-indexes 3 million chunks during office hours, and every other tenant’s p95 latency doubles. What is this called?
Shared compute means one tenant’s load affects others. Rate limits per tenant, off-peak jobs or a dedicated shard for large tenants help.
In a red-team test, 50 cross-tenant probes hit an endpoint missing the tenant filter. The ACL check lets 40% of foreign chunks through because group names repeat. How many cross-tenant leaks?
50 × 0.4 = 20. The ACL check helps but is not a tenant boundary; enforce the tenant separately.
A hospital’s records system removes a nurse from a ward at 10:02. The vector store syncs ACLs nightly at 02:00. Until when can she still retrieve that ward’s notes?
The index learns of the change only at the next sync. Syncing on change, by webhook, closes the gap to about a minute.
Which practices keep document permissions correct in a RAG system? Select all that apply.
Copy ACLs from the source system onto every chunk
Sync ACL changes by webhook or change feed
Store groups prefixed with the tenant id
Let the model decide which documents look confidential
Permissions come from the source system, stay fresh and are tenant-qualified. A model’s guess is not a permission.
A namespace-per-client store has a base p95 of 45 ms, and the in-query ACL filter adds 8 ms. What is the p95?
45 + 8 = 53 ms. Checking after retrieval would add about 30 ms instead, for the extra candidates.
A broker’s research assistant serves 12 large institutional clients with strict contracts and very different load. Which isolation fits best?
A shared index with a filter added in app code
A dedicated namespace, collection or shard per client
No isolation, since the research is similar
A few large, regulated clients justify dedicated partitions: stronger isolation, no noisy neighbours and easy erasure.
Which query keeps a Postgres RLS tenant policy but still returns a full top 10 when the ACL filter removes many HNSW candidates?
Sort by id instead of distance
Iterative index scans, added in pgvector 0.8, keep walking the index until enough rows pass the filter.
A payments SaaS moves its permission check from a prompt instruction into the query. Which change in a 500-probe forbidden-document red-team test is expected? Select all that apply.
The model never sees forbidden chunks
Stale-permission exposures from a nightly sync disappear
Cross-tenant leaks through an unfiltered endpoint necessarily disappear
In-query checks stop forbidden text reaching the model, but they are only as fresh as the ACL sync and are not a tenant boundary.
compress: How many bytes does a 1,024-dim float32 vector take?
The same vector as int8 takes?
What does product quantisation store per sub-vector?
A codebook id of its nearest centroid
One byte per sub-vector with 256 centroids.
Which encoding needs a training step?
PQ codebooks are learnt with k-means.
Which help recover recall after binary quantisation? Select all that apply.
Measuring against exact search to tune
For a top 10 with oversampling 4, how many candidates are rescored?
2 crore vectors at 128 bytes each need about?
Where can the original float32 vectors live when used only for rescoring?
Only a few dozen are read per query.
RAM costs ₹600 per GB-month. How much does 20.5 GB cost a month?
Few bits carry too little information.
Which are true of int8 scalar quantisation? Select all that apply.
Usually loses a point or two of recall
Needs a codebook of 256 centroids per sub-space
Clips values to a range first
Recall at 10 is 74% on 1,000 queries. How many true top-10 results were missed in total?
What is the main thing this technique changes?
Dimension reduction is a separate technique.
Recall stays low even with rescoring ×4. Next check?
Whether the model suits binary, or switch to int8
Some models lose too much at one bit.
PQ with 64 one-byte codes on 1,024 dims: compression versus float32?
Which vector stores offer built-in quantisation? Select all that apply.
Binary alone gives 74%; rescoring ×4 gives 96%. Gain in points?
What should a compression rollout report?
Recall at k against exact search, RAM and latency
choosevs: What should come first when choosing a vector store?
Hard constraints such as scale, residency and ops time
Constraints remove options before any test.
You already run Postgres and have 5 lakh vectors. A sensible first store?
Vectors must stay in the bank’s own cloud account. Which option is ruled out?
A managed service running in the vendor’s account
The data would leave its account.
What should a fair benchmark include? Select all that apply.
Self-hosted ₹40,000 + 16 h, staff ₹1,500 an hour. Total monthly cost?
Managed ₹55,000 + 2 h at ₹1,500 an hour. Total?
Why keep a nightly export of vectors and metadata?
To make a later migration a reload
Why can a public benchmark give the wrong answer for you?
Which family adds vectors to an existing keyword search cluster?
A team has no operations staff and no residency rule. Which family fits best?
Which are operations costs of self-hosting? Select all that apply.
p95 is 60 ms and the target is 50 ms. By how many ms does it miss?
Growth of 3× from 1 crore vectors means planning for?
Which is NOT part of this technique?
Index tuning is covered by the HNSW technique.
How many finalists should you usually benchmark?
Which measurements belong in the benchmark report? Select all that apply.
Two teams each pick a different new vector database. Main risk?
Two systems to run and secure
Filtered search behaves very differently across stores. So the benchmark must?
A store costs ₹45,000 a month at 1 crore. Roughly per lakh vectors?
Where is the residency rule checked?
Before the benchmark, as a hard constraint
It can rule options out at once.

ivf.q: In your own words: how does an IVF index make search faster, and what does it give up?
pts: scan only the nearest few lists
ivf.model: IVF groups the vectors into clusters with k-means and stores each vector in the list of its nearest centroid. A query is compared with the centroids, which is cheap, and only the closest few lists (the probes) are scanned with exact distances. It gives up some recall: a true neighbour that sits just across a cluster border, in a list that was not probed, is never seen. Raising probes buys recall back at the cost of speed.

ivf.q: A pgvector IVFFlat index was great at launch and is worse six months later. What happened, and what would you do?
pts: new data drifts or lists become unbalanced
ivf.model: The centroids were learned from the data present when the index was built. As new rows arrive with different content, they are forced into the nearest existing lists, some lists grow very large and borders no longer match the data, so recall and speed both fall. Measure recall against exact search, raise probes as a stopgap, and rebuild the index (REINDEX) on representative data. If data keeps arriving continuously, consider HNSW, which needs no training.

ivf.q: How would you choose lists and probes for 9 million rows, and how would you know you had them right?
ivf.model: pgvector suggests lists ≈ √rows above one million rows, so √9,000,000 = 3,000 lists, and probes ≈ √lists as a starting point, about 55. Then take a few hundred real queries, compute their true top 10 with exact search, and raise probes until recall@10 meets the target while latency stays within budget.

hnsw.q: Explain how an HNSW search finds a nearest neighbour without scanning everything.
pts: greedy hops from an entry point
drop a layer at a time
candidate list ef_search at the bottom
hnsw.model: HNSW is a layered graph. The top layers hold few nodes with long links, and the bottom layer holds every vector with short links. A search starts at an entry point on the top layer, repeatedly hops to whichever neighbour is closer to the query, and when none is closer it drops to the next layer and continues. On the bottom layer it keeps a list of ef_search candidates rather than one, which recovers neighbours a purely greedy walk would miss, and returns the best k.

hnsw.q: Recall is 0.90 and the target is 0.97. Walk through what you would change, in order.
pts: then M or ef_construction with a rebuild
hnsw.model: Raise ef_search first, because it is a query-time setting: try 80, 160 and so on, and measure recall@10 and p95 latency at each. If recall plateaus before the target or latency runs out, rebuild with a larger M or ef_construction, which improves the graph but costs memory and build time. Check the filters production uses too, since strict filters can lower recall on their own.

hnsw.q: A bank wants HNSW over 50 million 768-dimension vectors. What memory would you budget, and what would make you reconsider?
pts: quantization or DiskANN if RAM is short
hnsw.model: The raw vectors take 50 million × 768 × 4 bytes ≈ 154 GB, and bottom-layer links at M = 16 add about 50 million × 32 × 4 bytes = 6.4 GB, so plan for roughly 160 GB plus headroom and replicas. If that RAM is too expensive, compress the vectors with scalar or binary quantization and rescore, or move to an SSD-resident index such as DiskANN.

diskann.q: In your own words: how does DiskANN search a billion vectors on one machine?
pts: graph and full vectors on SSD
compressed codes in RAM guide the walk
few hops or reads per query
diskann.model: DiskANN keeps a Vamana graph and the full-precision vectors on SSD, with each node’s vector and neighbour list together in one sector, and keeps only small PQ codes for every vector in RAM. A search walks the graph from a fixed entry point, using the in-RAM codes to decide which nodes to read next, a few at a time (the beam width). The graph needs few hops, so only tens of SSD reads are issued, and the full vectors in the sectors already read give exact distances for the final ranking.

diskann.q: When would you choose DiskANN over HNSW, and when not?
pts: not when data fits in RAM
diskann.model: Choose DiskANN when vectors times bytes exceeds the RAM you can afford, typically hundreds of millions to billions of vectors, and a few milliseconds of latency is acceptable. Do not choose it when the data fits comfortably in RAM, because in-memory HNSW is faster and simpler, or when only network-attached or spinning disks are available, since latency depends on fast random reads from local NVMe.

diskann.q: A DiskANN index has p50 latency of 30 ms and the target is 5 ms. What would you check?
pts: disk type: local NVMe vs network
cache of hot nodes or load
diskann.model: Check the storage first: on network block storage each round trip costs about a millisecond, so move to local NVMe. Then look at the number of round trips, which is roughly the candidate list size L divided by the beam width: widen the beam to issue more reads per trip, and lower L if recall has headroom. Cache more nodes near the entry point, and measure under realistic concurrent load, since queueing on the SSD raises latency.

las.q: Why search in several layers instead of one precise pass?
pts: precise scoring is expensive per item
cheap first layer shrinks the set
las.model: Precise scoring, such as full-precision distances or a cross-encoder, is expensive per item and cannot run over millions of items within a latency budget. A cheap first layer over compressed vectors narrows millions to about a thousand, and each later, more precise layer sees far fewer items. The expensive work runs on a handful of candidates, so results are nearly as good as a precise search at a fraction of the cost.

las.q: End-to-end recall is 0.84, but every later layer looks fine. Where is the problem, and how do you fix it?
pts: the first layer drops true matches
las.model: Later layers can only reorder what they receive, so the loss is almost certainly in the first layer: it is keeping too few candidates, and true neighbours are dropped before any precise scoring happens. Measure first-layer recall at several candidate counts, raise the count or the oversampling factor until it retains nearly all of the true top 10, and check that the extra candidates still fit the latency budget.

las.q: Design a layered search for 100 million 1,024-dimension chunks with a 50 ms budget.
pts: binary or quantized first layer in RAM
oversample and rescore with more precise vectors
measure recall and latency per layer
las.model: Keep binary codes in RAM (100 million × 128 bytes = 12.8 GB) and scan or index them to keep about 1,000 candidates. Rescore those with int8 vectors to 100, then fetch the 100 full-precision vectors from SSD for an exact ranking of the top 10 to 20. Finish with a cross-encoder on those few passages. Measure recall and latency after each layer on sample queries, and give the first layer enough candidates that it rarely drops a true match.

hybrid.q: In your own words: why run dense and sparse search together, and how are they combined?
hybrid.model: Dense search matches meaning, so it finds paraphrases but blurs exact codes, names and rare terms. Sparse search such as BM25 matches exact terms, so it finds “error 809” but misses different wording. Running both and fusing the two lists with reciprocal rank fusion, which adds 1 ÷ (k + rank) from each list, lifts documents that both methods found without having to compare their incompatible raw scores.

hybrid.q: A teammate proposes adding the cosine score to the BM25 score. What is wrong with that, and what would you do?
pts: use RRF or normalize with a weight
hybrid.model: Cosine similarity sits roughly between 0 and 1, while BM25 is unbounded and varies from query to query, so a raw sum is dominated by BM25 and means something different for every query. Use reciprocal rank fusion, which needs no calibration, or normalize each list, for example min–max, and combine with a weight α tuned on an evaluation set that mixes code-style and meaning-style queries.

hybrid.q: How do you make sure hybrid search never shows a user a document from another tenant?
pts: store tenant or role metadata per chunk
filter inside the database in both retrievers
never rely on the LLM or post-filtering
hybrid.model: Store tenant and access metadata with every chunk in both the vector and the keyword index, and apply the user’s filter inside the database in both retrievers, before ranking and before any result leaves it. Do not rely on filtering after ranking, which can leak or leave short pages, and never rely on the LLM to hide content from the prompt.

metafilter.q: Explain the difference between pre-filtering, post-filtering and filtered ANN, and when each fits.
pts: post-filtering drops results after a top-k search
pre-filtering scores the matching set exactly
filtered ANN checks the filter during the walk
metafilter.model: Post-filtering runs the vector search first and drops non-matching results, so on average only k × selectivity survive; it suits broad filters with some oversampling. Pre-filtering finds the matching ids first and scores them exactly, which is perfect for rare filters because the set is small, but slow for broad ones. Filtered ANN checks the condition while the index is walked, so every result matches and latency stays low for broad and medium filters. Engines such as Qdrant use payload indexes to estimate cardinality and pick exact scans for small sets automatically.

metafilter.q: A region filter matches 1% of 20 lakh chunks. Your search post-filters an ANN top 10. How many results do you expect, how many candidates would you need, and what would you do instead? Show the working.
pts: filter inside the search or pre-filter
metafilter.model: 20 lakh × 1% = 20,000 matching chunks. A top 10 holds 10 × 0.01 = 0.1 of them on average, so the list is almost always empty. To expect 10 survivors you would fetch 10 ÷ 0.01 = 1,000 candidates, and a rarer filter would need even more. Instead, pass the filter into the vector query so it is applied during the search, or score the 20,000 matching chunks exactly, which takes about 2 ms.

metafilter.q: After adding filters, handlers say some Maharashtra circulars never appear and a few queries have become slow. Diagnose both.
metafilter.model: Missing circulars point to metadata: some chunks say “Maharashtra”, others “MH”, or the field was never populated, and exact filters silently drop them. Normalise values at ingestion and backfill. Slow queries usually come from a broad filter being handled as an exact scan over most of the collection, or from a filtered field without an index, which forces a full scan. Index every filtered field, let filtered ANN handle broad filters, and track recall and latency separately for broad, medium and rare filters.

tenancy.q: In your own words: how do you keep each client’s and each user’s documents separate in one vector store?
tenancy.model: Tenant isolation and document permissions are two layers. The tenant is taken from the verified login token and enforced below the application code: a namespace or shard per tenant, or row-level security in Postgres, so a forgotten filter cannot leak. Each chunk also carries the tenant-qualified groups allowed to read it, copied from the source system, and that ACL filter runs inside the query so only allowed chunks are ranked. Revocations are synced on change, so a removed user loses access within a minute.

tenancy.q: LendStack has 400 NBFC clients and 2,400 permission revocations a day; a revoked user queries each lost document 0.05 times an hour. Compare nightly, hourly and on-change ACL sync. Show the working.
pts: 1,440 a day with a nightly sync
60 a day with an hourly sync
tenancy.model: Exposures ≈ revocations × query rate × average stale window. Nightly: 2,400 × 0.05 × 12 hours = 1,440 a day. Hourly: 2,400 × 0.05 × 0.5 = 60. On change, with about a minute of lag: 2,400 × 0.05 × 1/60 ≈ 2. On-change sync is often cheaper than hourly full crawls too, because it moves only what changed.

tenancy.q: A client of your SaaS leaves and asks for its data to be erased under India’s DPDP Act. How does your isolation model affect this, and what must be deleted?
pts: namespace or shard: drop it in one step
shared index: delete by tenant filter
tenancy.model: With a namespace or shard per tenant, erasure is one call, such as deleting the whole namespace, and takes minutes. In a shared index it is a delete by tenant filter across a large index, which is slower and needs a check that nothing is left; with row-level security it is a DELETE by tenant followed by vacuum. In every model, also clear caches, embeddings copied into evaluation sets and backups once their retention ends, and record the erasure in an audit log. This is an engineering view, not legal advice.

compress.q: Explain scalar, product and binary quantisation, and how to keep recall.
compress.model: Scalar quantisation maps each dimension to int8 (4× smaller). Product quantisation splits the vector into sub-vectors stored as codebook ids (tens of times smaller, needs training). Binary keeps one bit per dimension (32× smaller, Hamming distance). Keep the originals on SSD and oversample then rescore to win back recall.

compress.q: 2 crore vectors of 1,024 dims: RAM as float32 and as binary?
compress.model: float32: 2 crore × 4,096 B ≈ 81.9 GB. Binary: 2 crore × 128 B ≈ 2.56 GB.

compress.q: After switching to binary codes, users say search results got worse. What do you check?
compress.model: Measure recall at 10 against exact search. Check that rescoring with the original vectors is on and oversampling is 3–4×. If recall is still low, the embedding model may have too few dimensions for binary; use int8 instead.

choosevs.q: How would you choose a vector store for a new RAG product?
choosevs.model: List hard constraints: scale and growth, filters and hybrid, residency, latency target, operations budget and cost. Shortlist two families that meet them, benchmark both on your own data and logged queries with filters, and keep a nightly export so the choice can be reversed.

choosevs.q: Self-hosted: ₹40,000 + 16 h; managed: ₹55,000 + 2 h; staff cost ₹1,500 an hour. Which is cheaper in total?
choosevs.model: Self-hosted 40,000 + 24,000 = ₹64,000; managed 55,000 + 3,000 = ₹58,000. Managed is cheaper by ₹6,000 if residency allows it.

choosevs.q: A team wants to adopt the store that topped a public benchmark. What do you say?
choosevs.model: Public benchmarks use other data, filters and hardware. Check the hard constraints first, then run both finalists on your own data and logged queries with filters, recording recall, p95, cost and operations hours.

cases.title: The assistant that used to find things
cases.brief: A general insurer's claims desk searches 40 million chunks of policy wordings, endorsements, regulator circulars and past claim notes, and an assistant drafts an answer for the handler. Handlers say it used to work and now misses obvious documents. It is one internal team on one corpus, the store has been running for two years, and handlers accept a three-second answer because a model writes it anyway.
evidence: The index is IVFFlat, built two years ago on the first 5 million chunks. About 25,000 new chunks arrive daily. Against exact search on 500 sample queries, recall@10 is now 0.78.
Of 800 failed searches reviewed by hand, 34% contain exact tokens - policy numbers, claim IDs, clause references such as “clause 4.3” or “MOT-2024-118734” - which the embeddings blur.
29% carry implicit filters: “motor own-damage claims in Pune above ₹2 lakh last quarter, flood related”. The system ignores the city, the amount and the date entirely.
The search server has 256 GB of RAM. 40 million vectors at 1,024 float32 dimensions is about 164 GB, plus roughly 5 GB of graph links.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.hnsw: Start here, because “it used to work” is the diagnosis. IVFFlat clusters were trained on the first 5 million chunks and 25,000 new ones arrive daily, so the data has drifted away from the clusters and recall has decayed to 0.78 - and that number is the ceiling on everything else, since a document the index never returns cannot be re-ranked or filtered into view. HNSW needs no training step and handles continuously growing data, and symptom 4 says it fits: 164 GB of vectors plus 5 GB of links against 256 GB of RAM.
why.hybrid: 34% of failures turn on policy numbers and clause references, which embeddings blur by design. Run keyword search alongside the vector index and fuse by rank rather than raw score, since scores from the two methods are not comparable. Oversample before filtering so the fusion does not leave you with too few results.
why.metafilter: 29% of queries carry hard facts - city, amount, date, claim type - that are currently being ignored, which means the assistant is answering a different question from the one asked. Make them indexed filter conditions rather than hints in a prompt, normalise the metadata first because “MH” and “Maharashtra” will silently drop matches, and choose pre- or post-filtering by how selective each filter is.
why.las: Useful, and the three-second budget is what makes it affordable: a cheap first pass over many candidates followed by a precise rescore raises precision without breaching latency. Note the risk - anything the first layer misses is lost for good - which is another reason to fix base recall first.
why.compress: Useful as headroom rather than a need: 164 GB fits in 256 GB today, but 25,000 chunks a day will not fit forever. Quantise when you must, keep the original vectors so rescoring stays possible, and measure recall against exact search rather than reporting the speed-up.
why.ivf: Not needed - it is the current index and the cause of symptom 1. Rebuilding it on the full 40 million would help for a while and then drift again, because the training step is a snapshot and this corpus grows every day.
why.diskann: Not needed on these numbers, and the arithmetic is the whole argument: 169 GB fits inside 256 GB of RAM, where DiskANN is slower than in-memory HNSW. It is the right answer at a scale this corpus has not reached.
why.tenancy: Not needed: one internal claims team on one corpus. There is no second client whose chunks must be kept apart, and no per-tenant erasure obligation in this evidence.
why.choosevs: Not needed: the store is not the problem, the index configuration and the missing filters are. Migrating databases mid-quarter would spend the whole quarter and fix none of the four symptoms.

firstWhy.hybrid: The right second step and the biggest reviewed slice at 34%. But fusing a keyword index with a vector index whose recall is 0.78 inherits that 0.78 on the vector side - you would be blending a good half with a decayed one, and then re-measuring everything after you fix the index anyway.
firstWhy.metafilter: The most clearly broken behaviour on the page, since the assistant is answering about the wrong city and nobody is told. It is also the cheapest to demonstrate. But a filter narrows a candidate set, and today the candidate set is already missing a fifth of what it should contain - filter a decayed recall and you get precise answers from an incomplete pool.
firstWhy.compress: Not wrong to plan, and you will need it within the year. But 164 GB fits in 256 GB today, so compressing now trades recall for memory you are not short of - and it would be measured against a baseline index that is itself broken.

cases.model: Start by replacing the IVFFlat index with HNSW, because the complaint is decay rather than design: clusters trained on the first 5 million chunks with 25,000 arriving daily have drifted, recall@10 has fallen to 0.78 against exact search, and that number caps every later improvement - nothing can re-rank or filter a document the index never returns. The arithmetic supports it, 164 GB of vectors plus about 5 GB of links inside 256 GB of RAM, and HNSW needs no training step for continuously growing data. Next add hybrid search for the 34% of queries carrying policy numbers and clause references, fusing by rank rather than raw score and oversampling before any filter. Then turn the implicit filters into real ones: index city, amount, date and claim type, normalise the values first since “MH” and “Maharashtra” will silently drop matches, and pick pre- or post-filtering per filter by selectivity. With a three-second budget there is room for a coarse-to-fine final rescore. Compression is headroom for next year rather than a need today; DiskANN is for a scale this corpus has not reached; the store itself is fine, and there is one tenant.
cases.note: Every number here argues for in-memory HNSW and against DiskANN, and in Case 3 the identical reasoning points the other way on a corpus twenty times the size. The techniques do not change; the arithmetic decides.

hnsw: Symptom 1 is the shape of the whole complaint: an index trained two years ago on an eighth of today's data, 25,000 new chunks a day, and recall@10 down to 0.78 against exact search. Handlers say it used to work. What property of the current index explains a decay rather than a flaw?

The current index learned a structure once, from a snapshot. You want one that needs no training step and copes with data that keeps arriving - and symptom 4 is there to tell you whether you can afford it.
HNSW Index. Check its memory expectation against symptom 4's numbers, and read the pitfall about strict metadata filters, because your third step will meet it.
hybrid: Symptom 2: 34% of failed searches contain policy numbers, claim IDs and references like “clause 4.3”, and the embeddings blur them. The other failures are about meaning. How do you serve both at once?
Run both kinds of search and combine the results - and be careful how you combine them, because the two methods' scores are not on the same scale.
Hybrid Search. Read the pitfall about raw scores not being comparable, and the one about post-filtering leaving too few results.
metafilter: Symptom 3: “motor own-damage claims in Pune above ₹2 lakh last quarter”, and the system ignores the city, the amount and the date. Those are not preferences to be matched approximately - they are conditions. What makes them conditions?

Stop asking the prompt to respect them and make them a guaranteed part of the query. Then worry about whether to apply them before or after the vector search, and about whether the values are even consistent.
Metadata Filtering. All three pitfalls matter here: post-filtering a small top-k, pre-filtering something broad, and inconsistent values like “MH” versus “Maharashtra”.

drop.ivf: IVFFlat is what is running now. Rebuilding it on all 40 million chunks would lift recall - for how long, given 25,000 new chunks a day and a training step that is a snapshot?
drop.diskann: DiskANN exists for indexes that do not fit in memory. Do the arithmetic in symptom 4: how much RAM does this index need, and how much does the server have?
drop.tenancy: Multi-tenancy keeps one client's vectors away from another's. How many clients are searching this corpus?
drop.choosevs: Choosing a vector store is the decision you make at the start or when you have genuinely outgrown one. Which of these four symptoms is caused by the database rather than by how it is configured?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Now ask what every other fix is multiplied by: re-ranking, filtering and fusing all operate on the candidates the index returns, and today it returns 78% of what it should.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Recall@10 is 0.78, and a document the index never returns cannot be filtered, fused or re-ranked into view.
29% of queries are silently answered about the wrong city, amount and date, which is the most misleading behaviour here.
34% of reviewed failures contain exact tokens, which is the largest measured slice of the failures.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the other fixes act on. Filters and fusion both work over the candidate set the index hands back, so improving them while that set is a fifth short produces precise answers drawn from an incomplete pool - and you would have to re-measure all of it after fixing the index anyway. Base recall is the ceiling; raise the ceiling first.

cases.title: The search that showed one client another client's loan files
cases.brief: A lending-SaaS vendor runs document search for 1,400 client NBFCs out of one vector store: loan files, KYC packs, credit memos. Each client's users should see only their own documents, and within that only what their group may open. A client reported seeing a chunk that was not theirs, and the vendor's security review is now open.
evidence: The tenant filter is added by hand in application code. A new export endpoint shipped last month without it, and that is how one client saw another client's chunks.
A nightly ACL sync means a revoked user keeps read access for up to a day. A departed employee used the search the morning after their last day.

Group names such as “credit-ops” exist in many tenants, so an ACL check that matches on group alone passes other tenants' chunks. Rare filters post-applied to a top 10 also leave the smallest clients two or three results.
Each tenant has its own HNSW index - 1,400 graphs - and heavy per-tenant deletes have degraded many of them. The box is out of RAM and recall is falling unevenly across clients.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.tenancy: Start here, and it is not close. Three of the four symptoms are this one technique done by hand: a tenant filter living in application code will be forgotten on the next endpoint, which is exactly what happened; a group name shared across tenants means an ACL check alone is not isolation; and a nightly sync is a day-long window on revoked access. Enforce the tenant boundary where it cannot be skipped rather than in each call site, scope ACL checks within a tenant, and make revocation immediate.
why.metafilter: The other half of symptom 3 is ordinary filtering done wrongly: a rare filter post-applied to a top 10 returns two or three results, which is why the smallest clients see a near-empty search. Pre-filter or oversample by selectivity, and index the filter fields - and note that the tenant key is the most selective filter you have, so these two techniques meet here.
why.hnsw: 1,400 separate graphs with heavy per-tenant deletes is the documented way to degrade HNSW, and it is why recall is falling unevenly - some clients' graphs are far worse than others. Rebuild or compact them on a schedule rather than never, and reconsider one index with a mandatory tenant filter instead of 1,400 graphs, which is also what is exhausting the RAM.
why.compress: Useful because the box is out of RAM now: quantise to buy headroom, keep the original vectors so a precise rescore stays possible, and measure recall per tenant rather than overall, since this evidence shows per-tenant variance is the thing that hides problems.
why.choosevs: Useful as the question behind symptom 1: a store with a first-class tenant primitive would make the boundary structural instead of something application code must remember. Worth evaluating, but a migration is not how you close an open security review this month.
why.ivf: Not needed: nothing here points at cluster drift, and a training step per tenant across 1,400 collections would be worse on every axis than what they have.
why.diskann: Not needed: the problem is 1,400 graphs and unbounded deletes, not a single index too large for memory. Moving to disk would slow every client's search without touching the isolation failures.
why.las: Not needed: no symptom is about precision or latency. A coarse-to-fine pipeline would add layers to a system whose results are wrong for reasons of authorisation, not ranking.
why.hybrid: Not needed on this evidence: nothing says exact tokens are being missed. Adding a second index to keep in sync, in a system that already cannot keep a tenant filter in sync, would make the real problem worse.

firstWhy.metafilter: Genuinely half of the answer, and the two overlap - the tenant key is just the most important filter. But the smallest clients seeing three results is a quality complaint, while one client seeing another's loan files is a breach, and fixing filter selectivity does nothing about the endpoint that forgot the filter entirely.
firstWhy.hnsw: The box is out of RAM and recall is visibly falling, so this is pressing and it is your third step. It is also the one that most tempts a redesign - and if you rebuild the index layout before deciding how isolation is enforced, you will rebuild it again when the answer turns out to be one index with a mandatory filter.
firstWhy.choosevs: The best strategic read on the page: a store with a native tenant primitive would make symptom 1 structurally impossible. But a migration takes a quarter or more, and there is an open security review and a live cross-tenant exposure right now.

cases.model: Start with multi-tenancy and access control, because three of the four symptoms are that one concern handled by hand. Move the tenant boundary out of application code and into something the query path cannot bypass, so a new endpoint cannot ship without it; scope every ACL check within a tenant, since group names like “credit-ops” exist in many of them and matching on group alone is not isolation; and replace the nightly ACL sync with immediate revocation, because a day of read access after an employee leaves is a day too long. Then fix ordinary filtering: pre-filter or oversample by selectivity so a rare filter post-applied to a top 10 stops leaving small clients with three results, and index the filter fields. Next address the index layout - 1,400 HNSW graphs with heavy per-tenant deletes is the documented path to a degraded graph, so compact on a schedule and seriously consider one index with a mandatory tenant filter, which also addresses the RAM. Quantise for headroom, keeping original vectors and measuring recall per tenant rather than overall. A store with a native tenant primitive is worth evaluating but not while a security review is open; and IVF, DiskANN, re-ranking layers and a second keyword index all address problems this system does not have.
cases.note: Case 1's fix was recall and this one's is authorisation, and the difference shows up in what “wrong result” means: there it was a document missing, here it is a document that should never have been reachable. Read who is allowed to see what before tuning how well it is found.

tenancy: Symptoms 1, 2 and 3 share a cause. A filter written by hand in app code was forgotten on a new endpoint, a nightly sync leaves revoked users reading for a day, and a group name that exists in many clients passes other clients' chunks. What single concern is all of that?

Not about relevance at all - about one store serving many client companies and never letting one reach another's data, or letting a revoked user keep reading. The clue is that none of these three failures was a ranking mistake.
Multi-Tenancy and Access Control. All three pitfalls are literally in this evidence: the hand-added filter forgotten on one endpoint, the shared group name, and the nightly sync window.
metafilter: The second half of symptom 3: a rare filter applied after a top-10 search leaves the smallest clients with two or three results. What is going wrong mechanically, and what are the two ways round it?
Think about when the condition is applied relative to the vector search, and about how selective the condition is. Also ask whether the fields are indexed and the values consistent.
Metadata Filtering. Read the pitfalls about post-filtering a top 10 with a rare filter and about pre-filtering something broad - the choice depends on selectivity.
hnsw: Symptom 4: 1,400 separate graphs, heavy per-tenant deletes, a box out of RAM, and recall falling unevenly from client to client. What does this index type do under heavy deletion, and what does 1,400 of them cost?
The structure here is a graph that is built once and then edited. Edits - especially deletions - do not leave it as good as they found it, and the memory expectation is per index.
HNSW Index. Read the pitfall about heavy deletes and updates degrading the graph, and the one about memory, then reconsider whether 1,400 indexes was the right layout.

drop.ivf: IVFFlat trains clusters on a snapshot of the data. What would that mean across 1,400 tenant collections, and which of these symptoms would it fix?
drop.diskann: DiskANN is for one index too large for memory. Is this index too large, or are there simply 1,400 of them with unbounded deletes?
drop.las: Coarse-to-fine retrieval buys precision within a latency budget. Which symptom here is about precision or latency, rather than about who is allowed to see a document?
drop.hybrid: Hybrid search adds a keyword index alongside the vector one. Which symptom says exact tokens are being missed - and what does this team's track record with keeping a filter in sync suggest about maintaining two indexes?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right, and two of your choices are the same idea at different stakes - a tenant key is a filter, but it is the filter that must never be optional. Order by what happens when each one is wrong.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: The box is out of RAM and recall is already falling unevenly across clients, so capacity is the live operational failure.
A tenant boundary enforced by hand in application code has already leaked one client's loan files to another, and will be forgotten again.
The smallest clients get two or three results from a rare filter, which is the most common day-to-day complaint.
whyFirst.why: Order by what is not recoverable. A degraded graph and a thin result set are both fixable with nobody outside the company any the wiser; one NBFC seeing another's loan files cannot be un-seen, has already happened, and will happen again on the next endpoint somebody forgets. Make the boundary impossible to bypass, then make the search good.

cases.title: The catalogue search that outgrew its RAM budget
cases.brief: A marketplace searches 1.2 billion vectors across product titles, descriptions and review text, behind an 80 ms latency target and an expensive cross-encoder that re-ranks the final candidates. The catalogue is public, there is one corpus and no per-client isolation to worry about. The infrastructure bill has become the loudest problem in the room, and the last attempt to cut it quietly cost a third of the recall.
evidence: 1.2 billion vectors at 768 float32 dimensions is about 3.4 TB. In-memory HNSW would need a fleet of 28 high-memory nodes; the RAM bill is ₹71 lakh a month and rising with the catalogue.
A binary-quantisation experiment cut memory 32-fold, and recall@10 fell from 0.94 to 0.61. The original vectors were not retained, so a precise rescore was impossible.
The team reports a 9× speed-up from the quantised index. Recall against exact search on the live corpus has never been measured; the 0.61 came from a one-off offline sample.
First-stage retrieval is a single pass and the cross-encoder only ever sees its top 50, so anything the first pass misses is gone for good.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.diskann: Start here, because the constraint is structural: 3.4 TB will not sit in RAM at any sensible price, and ₹71 lakh a month for 28 nodes is the bill for pretending otherwise. DiskANN is built for hundreds of millions to billions of vectors with millisecond targets, which is this workload described exactly - and the 80 ms budget is comfortably inside what it delivers. Budget for a long index build and good SSDs, both of which it depends on.
why.compress: Essential, and essential to do properly - symptom 2 is what doing it carelessly looks like. Binary quantisation on an unsuited model collapsed recall from 0.94 to 0.61, and because the original vectors were discarded there was no way to rescore and recover. Keep the full-precision vectors, choose the quantisation level by measured recall, and oversample candidates when searching compressed ones.
why.las: The single-pass first stage is why a quantisation mistake was unrecoverable: whatever the coarse layer misses never reaches the cross-encoder. Make the pipeline explicitly coarse-to-fine - a wide cheap pass over compressed vectors, a rescore against the retained full-precision vectors, then the cross-encoder - and widen the first stage, because its recall is the ceiling on the whole chain.
why.metafilter: Useful and, in a marketplace, eventually unavoidable: category, price band, availability and seller rating are hard conditions. Not in the first three only because no symptom here reports a filter failing - but index them properly when you do, and watch the interaction between strict filters and graph paths.
why.hybrid: Useful: shoppers type SKUs, brand names and model numbers that embeddings blur, so a keyword half would pay for itself. Secondary to being able to serve the corpus at all within budget.
why.ivf: Not needed: a continuously growing catalogue is the worst case for an index whose clusters are trained on a snapshot, and it does nothing about 3.4 TB.
why.hnsw: Not needed, and this is the instructive one: HNSW is the right default and it is exactly what does not work here, because it expects the vectors and the graph in RAM. At 3.4 TB that is 28 nodes and ₹71 lakh a month - the same arithmetic that made HNSW correct in Case 1 rules it out at twenty times the scale.
why.tenancy: Not needed: a public catalogue with one corpus and no client boundaries. There is nothing to isolate.
why.choosevs: Not needed now: at this scale a migration is a year of work, and the failures are in the index type, the compression and the pipeline shape rather than in the database. Revisit if your store cannot offer a disk-based index at all.

firstWhy.compress: The right instinct about cost and your second step - but symptom 2 is what happens when compression is the whole plan. Squeezing 3.4 TB into RAM by making vectors 32 times coarser is what cost a third of the recall; decide where the index lives first, and compression becomes a tuning choice rather than a desperate one.
firstWhy.las: The sharpest diagnosis on the page - a single-pass first stage is why the recall loss was unrecoverable - and it is what makes the other two safe. But a rescore layer needs the precise vectors to rescore against and an index that can serve a wide first pass, and neither exists yet.
firstWhy.hybrid: Shoppers do type SKUs and model numbers, so this would help, and it is independent work that can run in parallel. As a first move it improves the ranking of a system whose real problem is that serving the corpus at all costs ₹71 lakh a month.

cases.model: Start with DiskANN, because the governing fact is that 3.4 TB of vectors cannot live in RAM at a defensible price, and 28 high-memory nodes at ₹71 lakh a month is the cost of insisting. DiskANN is designed for exactly this - hundreds of millions to billions of vectors with millisecond latency - and the 80 ms target sits well inside it; plan for a long index build and good SSDs, which it depends on. Then redo compression properly: choose the quantisation level by measured recall rather than by the memory saving, keep the full-precision vectors so a rescore is possible, and oversample candidates when searching compressed ones - the collapse from 0.94 to 0.61 happened because binary quantisation was applied blind and the originals were thrown away. Make the pipeline explicitly coarse-to-fine, widening the first pass and rescoring against the retained vectors before the cross-encoder, since a single-pass first stage is what made the earlier mistake unrecoverable. Start measuring recall against exact search on the live corpus rather than reporting speed-ups from an offline sample. Add hybrid search for SKUs and model numbers, and index the category and price filters when you need them. HNSW is the usual default and is precisely what the arithmetic rules out here.
cases.note: The arithmetic in Case 1 made in-memory HNSW right and DiskANN wrong; the same arithmetic at twenty times the scale reverses both. And note what the three cases punished: a decayed index, a boundary enforced by convention, and a saving taken without measuring what it cost.

diskann: Symptom 1 is one calculation and one bill: 1.2 billion vectors, about 3.4 TB, 28 high-memory nodes, ₹71 lakh a month, against an 80 ms target. What index type exists because the index does not fit in memory?

The usual in-memory default assumes vectors and graph both live in RAM. There is an alternative designed for billions of vectors, with latency measured in milliseconds rather than microseconds - and it cares about two things you must budget for.
DiskANN. Read the pitfalls about index build time and SSD quality, and note what it is worse than at small scale.
compress: Read symptoms 2 and 3 together: binary quantisation cut memory 32-fold and recall fell from 0.94 to 0.61, the originals were discarded so nothing could be rescored, and the team reports a 9× speed-up having never measured recall on the live corpus. What is the technique, and what are the three ways they misused it?
The right idea executed carelessly. Look at what must be retained, what must be oversampled, and what must be measured before any saving is claimed.

Vector Compression. Its three pitfalls are symptoms 2 and 3 almost word for word: binary quantisation on an unsuited model, compressing without keeping the originals, and reporting speed-ups without measuring recall.
las: Symptom 4: one first-stage pass, a cross-encoder that only sees its top 50, and anything missed early is gone for good. What shape of pipeline is this - and what is the fix for the recall loss in symptom 2 being unrecoverable?
Several layers, cheapest first, each narrowing for the next, with a precise rescore before the expensive final model. The key question is how wide the first layer is.
Coarse-to-Fine Retrieval and Re-scoring. The first pitfall - anything the first layer misses is lost for good - is symptom 4, and it is why your compression step must keep the precise vectors.

drop.ivf: IVFFlat trains its clusters on a snapshot. What happens to that on a catalogue that grows continuously - and what does it do about 3.4 TB?
drop.hnsw: HNSW is the general-purpose default and expects vectors and graph in RAM. Read symptom 1's arithmetic: what does that expectation cost here?
drop.tenancy: Multi-tenancy keeps one client's data from another's. How many clients does a public marketplace catalogue have?
drop.choosevs: Choosing a vector store is a decision for the start of a project or a genuine outgrowing. Which symptom here was caused by the database rather than by the index type, the compression or the pipeline?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right and they depend on each other in one direction. Ask which decision the other two are configuring: compression level and rescore layers are both properties of an index whose home you have not chosen yet.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A single-pass first stage is why the earlier recall loss could not be recovered, so the pipeline shape is the root cause.
3.4 TB cannot sit in RAM at a defensible price, so where the index lives determines how much you must compress and what you can rescore against.
Recall fell from 0.94 to 0.61 and has never been measured on the live corpus, so measurement must come before any change.
whyFirst.why: Order from the constraint that sets the others. Measurement is a discipline to adopt immediately rather than a step in the sequence, and the pipeline shape is what makes the compression safe - but both are decisions about an index, and the reason compression turned desperate was the attempt to force 3.4 TB into memory. Choose where the index lives and compression becomes a tuning dial instead of a 32-fold gamble.

quiz: 5 million vectors, a p95 target under 20 ms, high recall needed, and enough RAM. Which index?
HNSW is the low-latency, high-recall default when vectors and graph fit in memory.
An IVFFlat index was created on an empty table; after loading data, recall is terrible. Why?
The clusters were learned from no data; rebuild after loading
IVF learns its centroids when the index is built. Build it after representative data is in the table.
HNSW recall is 0.88 against a 0.95 target, and latency has headroom. What do you change first?
ef_search is the query-time dial and needs no rebuild. Change M or ef_construction only if that isn't enough.
2 billion vectors, and the budget allows one server with 256 GB of RAM. Which approach?
Full vectors won't fit in RAM. DiskANN keeps compressed codes in RAM and full vectors on SSD.
The query “error 809 VPN” misses the one page that mentions error 809. What's the fix?
The exact code needs keyword matching; hybrid search adds BM25 and fuses the rankings.
Dense search ranks D1 first; sparse search ranks it third. With k = 60, what is D1's RRF score?
Users type “2 BHK flats in Pune under 50 lakh” and results ignore the price. What's the fix?
A query optimization agent that extracts filters
Price, city and size are structured constraints. Extract them as filters instead of hoping vectors capture them.
In a multi-stage search, the binary first layer has recall@1000 of 0.80. What's the best final recall you can get?
It depends only on the last layer
Later layers can only reorder what the first layer returned. Misses there are permanent.
pgvector IVFFlat on 4 million rows. What value of lists is suggested?
Filtering to one tenant (0.1% of data) with HNSW returns too few results. Why, and what's the fix?
Filtering after the ANN search leaves few matches; pre-filter or partition by tenant
When filters are applied after the approximate search, most candidates are thrown away. Use filtered or partitioned search.

ivf.t: A pgvector table has 600,000 rows. What value of lists does pgvector suggest?
ivf.a: Up to 1M rows, lists ≈ rows ÷ 1,000 = 600. Start probes around √600 ≈ 24 and tune for recall.
iv: How does IVF trade recall for speed?
It scans only the closest few clusters (probes) instead of every vector. More probes raise recall and latency; a true neighbour in an unscanned cluster is missed.
When would you choose IVFFlat over HNSW?

When you need faster index builds and less memory, or rebuild from batch data regularly, and can accept slightly lower recall at the same speed. HNSW is usually better for low-latency, high-recall search.
mis: Building the index before loading data
Load representative data, then build
Never rebuilding after large changes
Rebuild when the data distribution drifts

hnsw.t: 1 million vectors with M = 16. The bottom layer keeps up to 2 × M = 32 links per node at 4 bytes each. Estimate the extra memory for those links, in MB.
hnsw.a: 32 links × 4 B × 1,000,000 nodes = 128 MB, on top of the raw vectors (1.5 GB at 384 float32 dims). Raising M raises this directly.
iv: Explain how HNSW search works.

Start at an entry point on the sparse top layer, greedily move to neighbours closer to the query, and when none is closer, drop a layer and repeat. The bottom layer holds every vector and is searched with a candidate list of size ef_search.
What do M, ef_construction and ef_search trade off?

M sets links per node (recall and memory), ef_construction sets the build-time candidate list (graph quality versus build time), and ef_search sets the query-time list (recall versus latency). Only ef_search changes without a rebuild.
mis: Raising M to fix recall at query time
Tune ef_search first; M needs a rebuild
Testing recall without your real filters
Benchmark with the filters production uses

diskann.t: 500 million vectors × 768 float32 dimensions. How much RAM for 64-byte compressed codes instead of full vectors, in GB?
diskann.a: Full vectors: 500M × 3,072 B ≈ 1.5 TB. Codes: 500M × 64 B = 32 GB in RAM, with the full vectors on SSD.
iv: How does DiskANN keep latency low while reading from SSD?

It navigates a graph in few hops using compressed vectors held in RAM, reads only a handful of SSD pages per query for full-precision vectors, and batches reads with beam search. Fast NVMe random reads make it practical.
When is DiskANN the wrong choice?
At small or medium scale where vectors fit in RAM (HNSW is faster), on slow disks, or when the index changes constantly without a streaming or fresh variant.
mis: Running it on network or spinning disks
Use local NVMe SSDs
Benchmarking one query at a time
Measure p95 latency under concurrent load

las.t: Layer 1 keeps 1,000 candidates with recall 0.97. Layer 2 keeps 100 and retains 0.99 of what it receives. Layer 3 keeps 10 and retains 0.95. End-to-end recall?
las.a: 0.97 × 0.99 × 0.95 ≈ 0.91. Each layer's losses multiply, so the weakest early layer caps the whole pipeline.
iv: Why use several retrieval stages instead of one precise search?
Precise scoring is expensive per item. A cheap first stage shrinks millions of items to hundreds, so the costly stages run on few items and results stay near-precise within the latency budget.
How do you size each stage?
Measure recall at several candidate counts per stage, pick the smallest count where the next stage rarely misses true matches, then check end-to-end recall and per-stage latency.
mis: Too few first-stage candidates
Oversample early; misses there are permanent
Tuning stages only in isolation
Measure end-to-end recall and latency

hybrid.t: Dense ranks A 1st, B 2nd, C 3rd. Sparse ranks C 1st, A 2nd, D 3rd. With k = 60, which document wins RRF?
hybrid.a: A: 1/61 + 1/62 ≈ 0.03252. C: 1/63 + 1/61 ≈ 0.03226. A wins narrowly; B and D, found by only one method, trail.
iv: Why fuse by rank instead of raw scores?
Cosine and BM25 scores sit on different, query-dependent scales, so adding them is meaningless without normalization. RRF uses only ranks, which are comparable and robust.
How do you enforce permissions in hybrid search?
Store access metadata (tenant, roles) with each chunk and filter inside the database before results leave it, ideally in both retrievers. Never rely on the LLM to hide content the user shouldn't see.
mis: Adding raw BM25 and cosine scores
Use RRF or normalize scores first
Filtering permissions after the LLM sees results
Filter in the database before results are returned

metafilter.t: A search post-filters its ANN results by region. The region filter matches 2% of chunks, and filter values are spread evenly. How many candidates must the ANN search fetch so that, on average, 10 survive the filter?
metafilter.a: Expected survivors = candidates × selectivity, so candidates = 10 ÷ 0.02 = 500. Fetching the usual 10 would leave 0.2 on average. At 0.2% selectivity you would need 5,000, which is why rare filters belong inside the search.
iv: Pre-filtering, post-filtering or filtered ANN: how do you choose?

Look at selectivity. Post-filtering is only safe for broad filters and needs oversampling of about k ÷ selectivity. Pre-filtering with an exact scan is ideal when few items match, because scoring 10,000 vectors is cheap. Filtered ANN, where the index checks the filter during the graph walk, covers the middle and broad cases. Engines such as Qdrant choose between exact and graph search from the estimated cardinality, so index the filtered fields and test recall per band.
Why can filtered HNSW lose recall, and how do engines fix it?

A strict filter removes most nodes, so the graph walk can hit dead ends where no matching neighbour is linked. Engines add filter-aware links when payload indexes exist before indexing, explore two hops (Weaviate's ACORN), keep scanning until enough rows pass (pgvector iterative scans), or switch to an exact scan of the matching ids when the set is small.
mis: Taking the top 10 and filtering in application code
Pass the filter into the vector query, or oversample by about 10 ÷ selectivity
Filtering on fields with no index or with inconsistent values
Index every filtered field and normalise values such as “MH” and “Maharashtra” at ingestion

tenancy.t: LendStack’s clients revoke 2,400 user–document permissions a day. A revoked user queries each lost document about 0.05 times an hour, and with a nightly ACL sync the average stale window is 12 hours. How many stale-permission exposures happen a day?
tenancy.a: 2,400 × 0.05 × 12 = 1,440 exposures a day. An hourly sync (average window 0.5 hours) gives 60; syncing on change, within about a minute, gives about 2.
iv: How would you isolate tenants in a shared vector store?

Pick the model by tenant size and risk: a namespace, collection or shard per tenant for large or regulated clients, and a shared index with a tenant index such as Qdrant’s is_tenant for many small ones, or row-level security if the vectors live in Postgres. In every case the tenant comes from the verified token and is enforced below the application code, so one forgotten filter cannot leak. Red-team it with cross-tenant queries before launch.
Why not just tell the model which documents the user may see?

A prompt instruction is not a permission check. Once forbidden text is in the context, prompt injection or a cleverly worded question can extract it. Enforce ACLs inside the query, before ranking, so forbidden chunks never reach the model, and keep the ACLs fresh by syncing on change from the source system.
mis: Checking permissions in the prompt or after the model answers
Filter by tenant-qualified ACLs inside the database query
Syncing ACLs nightly
Sync revocations on change with webhooks or change feeds, and alert on sync lag
