compress.t: 2 crore vectors of 1,024 dims are stored as binary codes (1 bit per dimension). How many GB of RAM do the codes need?
compress.a: 1,024 bits = 128 bytes per vector. 2 crore × 128 bytes = 2,56,00,00,000 bytes ≈ 2.56 GB, against 81.9 GB for float32.
iv: How does product quantisation work?

The vector is split into m sub-vectors. For each sub-space a codebook of 256 centroids is trained, and each sub-vector is stored as the one-byte id of its nearest centroid. Distances are approximated from lookup tables.
How do you win back recall after binary quantisation?
Oversample, for example fetch 40 candidates for a top 10 from the binary index, then rescore them with the original float32 vectors, which can live on SSD.
mis: Throwing away the original vectors
Keep them on SSD so candidates can be rescored
Judging compression on speed alone
Measure recall at k against exact search on real queries

choosevs.t: A self-hosted engine costs ₹40,000 a month plus 16 operations hours at ₹1,500 an hour. A managed store costs ₹55,000 plus 2 hours. How many ₹ a month cheaper is the cheaper option?
choosevs.a: Self-hosted: 40,000 + 16 × 1,500 = ₹64,000. Managed: 55,000 + 2 × 1,500 = ₹58,000. Managed is ₹6,000 a month cheaper.
iv: How would you choose a vector database?

Write down hard constraints (scale, filters and hybrid, data residency, operations budget, cost), shortlist two options that meet them, benchmark both on your own data and logged queries with filters, and keep an export path.
When is pgvector enough?
When you already run Postgres and the corpus is up to roughly a crore of vectors with moderate query load; you keep joins, transactions and one system to operate.
mis: Trusting a public benchmark
Benchmark on your own data, filters and hardware
Counting only the infrastructure bill
Add operations hours at a real hourly cost

gloss: ANN
Approximate nearest neighbour search: finds close vectors fast by accepting a small recall loss.
centroid
The average vector of a cluster; IVF compares queries with centroids first.
lists
In IVF, the number of clusters the vectors are divided into.
probes
In IVF, how many of the nearest clusters are scanned per query.
HNSW
Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a layered graph index for fast ANN search.
ef_search
HNSW's query-time candidate list size; higher means better recall and slower queries.
Vamana
The graph construction algorithm used by DiskANN.
product quantization
Compressing vectors by splitting them into sub-vectors and storing codebook IDs.
RRF
Reciprocal Rank Fusion: combines rankings by summing 1 ÷ (k + rank).
oversampling
Fetching more candidates than needed early so later stages can recover recall.
pre-filtering
Applying metadata filters before or during the vector search rather than after it.
self-querying
An LLM turns a request into a semantic query plus structured filters.
selectivity
The share of items that match a filter. A 0.5% filter keeps 10,000 of 20 lakh chunks; rarer filters need a different strategy.
post-filtering
Running the vector search first and dropping non-matching results afterwards. Expected survivors are k × selectivity, so rare filters return few results.
payload index
An index on a metadata field (keyword, number or date) that lets a vector database filter quickly and estimate how many items match.
filtered ANN
Approximate nearest-neighbour search that checks the filter while walking the index, so every result returned matches.
row-level security
A database feature that applies a policy to every query on a table, such as tenant_id = the current tenant, so rows from other tenants are never returned.
namespace
A named partition inside one vector index; queries and deletes run within one namespace, which suits one namespace per tenant.
ACL sync
Copying document permissions from the source system into the vector store’s metadata, nightly, hourly or on each change.
noisy neighbour
A tenant whose heavy load, such as a bulk re-index, slows searches for other tenants on shared infrastructure.
scalar quantisation
Mapping each float dimension to a small integer, usually int8, after clipping to a range.
binary quantisation
Keeping only the sign of each dimension, one bit, and comparing vectors by Hamming distance.
rescoring
Re-ranking candidates found with compressed vectors using the original full-precision vectors.
oversampling
Fetching more candidates than needed, such as 4 × k, so rescoring can recover the true top k.
residency requirement
A rule that data must stay in a given country, region or cloud account.
total cost of ownership
Infrastructure or service fees plus the staff time needed to run a system.

las.name: Re-ranking with Cross-Encoders

las.name: Metadata Filtering

las.name: Vector Compression (Scalar, Product and Binary Quantisation)

metafilter.name: Hybrid Search

metafilter.name: Agentic and Corrective RAG
metafilter.note: Agentic retrieval turns a user's words into a structured filter; metadata filtering is where that filter is enforced, and a wrong or unindexed filter silently drops the right chunks.

metafilter.name: Coarse-to-Fine Retrieval and Re-scoring

hnsw.name: Metadata Filtering
hnsw.note: A strict filter removes most HNSW nodes and can break graph paths; filter-aware links, two-hop exploration or an exact scan of the matching set keep filtered recall high.

hnsw.name: Multi-Tenancy and Access Control
hnsw.note: A restrictive tenant or ACL filter can cut paths through an HNSW graph; per-tenant graphs or iterative index scans keep a filtered top 10 full.

hnsw.name: Semantic Response Caching

gifs.choosevs: A table lists four vector store families: Postgres with pgvector, a self-hosted engine, a managed serverless store and an OpenSearch cluster. Columns check three hard constraints for 1 crore vectors: data stays in the company's own account, p95 latency of 50 ms or less, and 20 operations hours or less. pgvector misses latency and the managed store misses residency. Of the two that pass, the engine gives 20 ms at ₹40,000 a month against OpenSearch at 45 ms and ₹70,000, and the final step is to benchmark both on 1,000 real queries.
gifs.compress: Three bars show one 1,024-dimension vector stored as float32 (4,096 bytes), int8 (1,024 bytes) and binary (128 bytes). Binary codes for 2 crore product vectors fit in 2.6 GB of RAM and return the top 40 by Hamming distance in 5 ms; the float32 originals on SSD rescore those 40 into the final top 10. Recall at 10 is 74 percent for binary alone and 96 percent with rescoring, while RAM falls from 81.9 GB to 2.6 GB and the monthly cost from ₹49,140 to ₹2,380.
gifs.diskann: DiskANN keeps 32-byte PQ codes in RAM (32 GB instead of 3.1 TB for a billion vectors), beam-searches a Vamana graph reading 6 SSD sectors, then re-ranks with exact distances.
gifs.hnsw: A three-layer HNSW graph is searched from the sparse top layer down, hopping closer to the query at each layer, then layer 0 keeps ef_search candidates and returns the best.
gifs.hybrid: Dense and BM25 rankings for a VPN error query are fused with reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60), so D1 (0.0325) and D3 (0.0323), found by both lists, rise to the top.
gifs.ivf: k-means groups 32 vectors into 4 lists; the query is compared with the centroids, the 2 nearest lists are probed, and only their 16 vectors are scanned exactly.
gifs.las: Four layers narrow 1,000,000 candidates: a binary scan keeps 1,000, int8 keeps 100, float32 keeps 10 and a cross-encoder ranks them, retaining about 0.96 of the true top 10.
gifs.metafilter: An animated sketch of Suraksha General's vector index, drawn as grey dots with a handful of blue dots for the chunks that match the filter motor, Maharashtra, circular, effective from April 2025. A query star sits in the middle. First, post-filtering: a dashed red circle marks the 10 nearest chunks, none of them blue, and a card reports that 10 × 0.005 = 0.05 matches are expected, so 0 are left. Next, filtered ANN with a payload index: the grey dots fade and green lines run from the query to the 10 matching chunks, and a card reports 10 of 10 matching with 100% recall. Finally, a small bar chart shows how many matches survive in a post-filtered top 10: 5 at 50% selectivity, 0.5 at 5% and 0.05 at 0.5%.
gifs.tenancy: Animated scene, about 8 seconds. A query bar reads "Priya, client t042, group pune-credit", with the tenant taken from her login token. On the left, a grid of 30 chunks from a store shared by 400 NBFC clients, each labelled with its client number and group, such as "042 pune", "117 pune" and "305 ops". First, a tenant layer inside the database, labelled "RLS or namespace", fades out every chunk from other clients, leaving 10 from t042. Next, an ACL layer in the query, "acl && t042:pune-credit", fades out the t042 chunks from the Mumbai group, leaving 5 green chunks, and a result pill reads "top 5, all allowed, page full". A closing note compares ACL sync: a nightly sync allows about 1,440 stale-permission exposures a day, syncing on change about 2.
